author: Fowler
title: Targeting Task Relevance in Intermediate-Layer Knowledge Transfer for Compressing Language Models
abstract: Compressing large language models into smaller variants through layer-wise distillation—wherein a compact student model learns to reproduce the hidden representations of a larger teacher model across all intermediate layers—represents an important compression technique. Yet this approach faces significant obstacles: the student's limited capacity typically leads to underfitting, and the representations extracted from the teacher encompass substantial redundancy not germane to the specific downstream task. We introduce a method employing task-specific filtering mechanisms that operate at each layer to curate which hidden representations the student should absorb. These filters extract task-relevant knowledge while discarding unnecessary information in the teacher's representations, thereby narrowing the capacity disparity and improving student fitting. Experiments across continual pre-training and fine-tuning settings show consistent and pronounced performance gains relative to baseline distillation approaches. The proposed method addresses the knowledge mismatch challenge through selective attention to task-pertinent features during the transfer process.

author: Johnson
title: Addressing Gender Bias During Knowledge Distillation of Language Models Through Counterfactual Swapping
abstract: Language models achieve strong text generation performance, yet compression via knowledge distillation enables deployment in resource-limited environments. A significant concern is that these models often encode problematic associations, such as connecting specific genders to occupations without factual basis. Standard knowledge distillation without fairness considerations risks transferring or amplifying the teacher model's embedded biases into the distilled version. We introduce a method for reducing gender inequity during knowledge distillation by training toward fairness constraints. Our approach incorporates two modifications centered on counterfactual role reversal: adjustment of teacher logits and expansion of the training corpus. We assess gender polarity across vocations in generated text from distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models, showing significant mitigation of gender disparity with minimal reduction in performance. Importantly, we find that mitigating gender polarity in text generation does not necessarily benefit fairness in learned embeddings or downstream classification tasks.

author: Hill
title: Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning for Persistent Task Acquisition in Minecraft Environments
abstract: This work presents a system capable of continuous task learning that leverages knowledge accumulated across successive objectives while preserving previously acquired competencies. Knowledge transfer occurs through the development of composable behavioral modules designed to accomplish objectives within Minecraft, a complex and high-dimensional domain representing an open challenge in persistent learning. These behavioral modules are integrated into a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework through two mechanisms: (1) an array structure for organizing deep modules and (2) module distillation, an adaptation of policy distillation techniques for consolidating behavioral knowledge. Module distillation allows the framework to preserve prior learning efficiently and thereby facilitate scaling to extended task sequences by compressing and integrating multiple behavioral modules into a unified distilled representation. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that this approach surpasses standard Deep Q Networks in performance metrics and sample efficiency when applied to selected Minecraft tasks.

author: Walker
title: Learning to Guide: Meta-Driven Student Knowledge Transfer
abstract: We introduce a knowledge distillation framework integrating meta learning in which, unlike conventional distillation approaches with static teachers, the instructor network adapts throughout the distillation process. The proposed method enables the teacher to progressively refine its guidance capacity through observing how well the student performs, optimizing the transfer of knowledge via meta-learning updates. Additionally, we propose a staging mechanism that strengthens coordination between the outer optimization loop and the inner adaptation process in meta-learning schemes targeting refined inner-learner behavior. Evaluation across multiple datasets demonstrates that the approach achieves substantial gains relative to standard distillation techniques, exhibits reduced dependence on student model size and parameter configurations, and generalizes more readily across distinct problem domains and architectures.

author: Doyle
title: Knowledge Distillation for Recommendation Systems via Latent Extraction and Ranking Relaxation
abstract: Knowledge distillation has become prevalent in recommendation systems as a strategy for compressing large models (teacher) into smaller variants (student) that maintain effectiveness while reducing inference latency. Prior approaches concentrate primarily on enabling students to replicate teacher predictions with precision, yet they overlook that such outputs constitute an incomplete characterization of the teacher's knowledge. We introduce a framework for knowledge distillation in recommender systems that facilitates student models to absorb both the implicit information stored within the teacher and its explicit prediction signals. The framework comprises two complementary components: 1) Distillation Experts, which transfers implicit knowledge through a specialized expert assignment mechanism designed to efficiently convey the teacher's extensive information to capacity-constrained students, and 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation, which extracts knowledge from prediction outputs by accounting for flexible ranking relationships between recommended items. Empirical validation demonstrates that this approach exceeds existing state-of-the-art baselines, achieving performance levels matching or surpassing the teacher model while requiring substantially shorter inference duration.

author: Rhodes
title: Knowledge Distillation for Continual Language Learning
abstract: Maintaining performance across sequential language tasks presents a significant challenge in lifelong language learning (LLL), where degradation relative to joint multi-task training often occurs. We propose a straightforward yet effective approach employing knowledge distillation to address this issue and integrate readily into established LLL frameworks. The method introduces a teacher model that initially acquires competence on each incoming task, subsequently transferring learned representations to the student LLL model through distillation mechanisms. This facilitates improved task adaptation while preserving earlier acquired knowledge. Our findings demonstrate consistent gains over existing state-of-the-art approaches, with the performance gap between lifelong and multi-task settings notably reduced across both generative and classification benchmarks.

author: Mcclain
title: Internal Representation Distillation for Knowledge Transfer
abstract: In knowledge distillation, a smaller student network is typically optimized to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher network by learning from its output probabilities as soft-labels. Yet when the teacher network is substantially oversized, soft-label matching alone provides no assurance that the student will acquire the teacher's internal knowledge; the student's internal representations may diverge significantly despite matching the soft-labels well. Such divergence in internal structure can degrade the generalization advantages originally meant for transfer from teacher to student. We introduce an approach to distill the internal representations directly from large models including BERT into reduced versions thereof. Multiple formulations and corresponding algorithms for executing such distillation are developed. Evaluation on GLUE benchmark datasets demonstrates that incorporating internal representation distillation substantially outperforms approaches relying exclusively on soft-label distillation.

author: Miller
title: Transfer Learning via Distillation to Enhance Performance on Spoken Question Answering
abstract: Answering questions posed in spoken form presents significant difficulty, requiring deep comprehension of complex audio material. The quality of transcribed text from automatic speech recognition (ASR) substantially influences the development of question answering systems. Recent findings indicate that ASR systems produce transcripts with substantial errors, which substantially constrain the machine's capacity for understanding in spoken question answering contexts. We propose a novel framework utilizing distillation techniques. Our methodology establishes a training procedure that transfers knowledge distillation between audio documents and their textual equivalents. The core contribution involves leveraging a language model as a supervision source through distillation, enabling the student model to achieve improved accuracy by mitigating mismatches between system-generated and human-produced transcriptions. Results on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset show our approach achieves superior performance compared to several contemporary language models.

author: Henderson
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Single-Network Ensemble Compression
abstract: Ensemble methods combining multiple trained base-level networks typically achieve superior performance, yet their practical deployment is constrained by substantial memory demands and computational costs during inference on large-scale test corpora such as ImageNet. We introduce a compression technique to consolidate trained multi-model ensembles into a unified network through knowledge distillation and transfer from diverse teacher networks to a single student network. To extract and convey heterogeneous knowledge across different trained teacher models, we employ an adversarial training strategy that incorporates block-wise optimization objectives guiding the student network to assimilate teacher knowledge while simultaneously training a discriminator to differentiate student and teacher features. This adversarial approach yields three key benefits: (1) the student network incorporating discriminative learning achieves superior optimization relative to non-ensemble baselines; (2) single-pass inference enables rapid execution while maintaining or exceeding performance of standard multi-model ensembles; (3) student networks can acquire knowledge from teacher models with diverse architectural designs. Comprehensive evaluation across CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet validates the approach. On ImageNet, a ResNet-50 variant achieves top-1/5 errors of 21.79%/5.99%, surpassing the baseline model by 2.06%/1.14%. Implementation and trained networks are accessible at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Optimizing Teacher Networks to Facilitate Student Learning via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We introduce an approach to knowledge distillation that prioritizes developing teacher networks suitable for effective student learning. Rather than following conventional strategies that presume fixed, pretrained teachers and then adapt student models accordingly, our method optimizes teacher architectures while jointly training student branches to ensure the resulting representations align well with student learning needs. This inversion of the typical training paradigm targets teacher model optimization as the central concern; the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure then proceeds using conventional techniques. Consequently, most existing knowledge distillation methods can incorporate our approach to enhance student model performance regarding both accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm achieves strong accuracy across well-established knowledge distillation techniques paired with various teacher-student model combinations, including scenarios where the architectures differ substantially and no information about the student configuration is available during teacher network training.

author: Wagner
title: Intra-Model Knowledge Transfer for Language Understanding Tasks
abstract: Deep neural architectures have emerged as dominant approaches in language understanding, frequently achieving performance levels that rival or exceed human-level results across diverse benchmarks. This effectiveness stems from the capacity of these models to develop rich knowledge representations. Though numerous strategies have been developed for learning more effective representations, distillation methods demonstrate that leveraging soft probability distributions from pre-trained networks can enhance the training of other models. We introduce an approach wherein a network distills knowledge from its own soft target distributions, extracting multimode information from the embedding space adjacent to the softmax output layer. Due to computational constraints, the method employs an approximation of these probability distributions. We evaluate our approach on two core language understanding problems: language modeling and machine translation. Across both tasks, results demonstrate consistent gains in model performance.

author: Johnson
title: Transfer Risk Analysis for Wide Neural Networks: Student Learning from Imperfect Soft Targets and Temperature-Scaled Outputs
abstract: Student networks trained on soft outputs from a teacher network represent a widely adopted compression and knowledge transfer paradigm. Despite empirical success, theoretical foundations remain underdeveloped. Recent neural tangent kernel theory facilitates representing wide networks as linear models over randomly initialized feature spaces. This work provides a theoretical framework for analyzing student training under teacher guidance in the wide network regime. We establish a generalization bound on the linearized network model. A quantity measuring task-level training hardship, termed data inefficiency, is introduced. Using this measure, we demonstrate that high weighting toward teacher soft outputs aids optimization when the teacher is accurate. In the practical setting of an imperfect teacher, ground-truth labels provide corrective signal for teacher mistakes, illuminating why practitioners combine ground-truth and soft targets in training.

author: Gonzalez
title: Supervise All Intermediate States: Knowledge Distillation through Dual-Instructor Collaboration
abstract: Resource scarcity and computational overhead limit deep neural network implementation on edge devices. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a lightweight student network to acquire knowledge from an expansive pre-trained teacher network. Yet conventional knowledge distillation approaches overlook the informative signals present during the learning trajectory itself. This work introduces a method employing two distinct instructors for knowledge transfer. A freshly-initialized instructor (from-scratch instructor) sequentially supervises the student by providing intermediate logits, ensuring the student follows a high-accuracy trajectory to the ultimate predictions. Concurrently, a pre-existing instructor (domain-expert instructor) directs the student's attention toward task-relevant regions that maximize performance. Synthesizing guidance from both instructors yields marked improvements in student network efficacy. Validation across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet demonstrates that this knowledge distillation approach is both effective and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

author: Santos
title: Attention-Based Channel Transfer in Student-Teacher Network Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A student network can acquire knowledge from a teacher network to achieve comparable accuracy with substantially fewer parameters and computational demands. We introduce three components for this transfer process: a channel-focused attention mechanism for propagating channel-level information, a variant that constrains student learning to only correct predictions rather than full probability distributions, and a scheduling approach that progressively reduces distillation loss influence to shift optimization control toward the student. The channel-wise attention component directly conveys channel representations from teacher to student. The prediction-constrained variant differs from standard distillation by limiting the student to match only accurate outputs instead of the teacher's entire predictive distribution across samples. Progressive weight reduction in the distillation objective gradually transfers the optimization burden from teacher toward student. Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR100 demonstrate effectiveness. ResNet18 achieves 27.68% top-1 error on ImageNet, exceeding prior state-of-the-art results. On CIFAR100, the student network surpasses teacher performance. Implementation details are available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Distillation for Adversarial Defense
abstract: Classification via neural networks benefits from knowledge distillation to compress large architectures into compact, performant variants, yet these compact networks exhibit susceptibility to adversarial perturbations. This work examines whether and how teacher robustness against adversarial examples transfers to students through the distillation process. We demonstrate that students can acquire substantial robustness from teachers via distillation on unperturbed training data alone. Third, we propose a method enabling transfer of adversarial robustness to student architectures during distillation. Beyond achieving the small model size and high clean accuracy typical of standard distillation, this approach additionally conveys the enhanced robustness inherent in teacher networks to their student counterparts. Experimental results reveal that students trained with this method substantially exceed adversarially trained networks of matching architecture in robust accuracy metrics, establishing new benchmarks on established evaluation protocols for adversarial robustness. As a final contribution, we integrate expedited adversarial training techniques into this framework to enable faster distillation with adversarial robustness.

author: Robinson
title: Understanding Deep Learning Through the Lens of Ensemble Methods, Self-Distillation, and Knowledge Transfer
abstract: This work provides formal analysis of how combining independently trained neural networks can boost test accuracy and how such gains transfer to individual models via knowledge distillation. We focus on the scenario where multiple models share identical architecture and training procedure but diverge only through initialization randomness, examining averaged output combinations. The observed phenomenon departs fundamentally from classical learning frameworks including boosting and neural tangent kernel theory. We establish a theoretical foundation by introducing multi-view structured data, under which independently trained networks demonstrably attain higher test performance. Furthermore, superior predictive capability can be rigorously transferred to a single model by optimizing it to replicate ensemble outputs rather than ground-truth labels. This perspective reveals ensemble behavior in deep networks through mechanisms entirely distinct from conventional theory, exposing how ensemble outputs encode implicit knowledge amenable to transfer via distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that self-distillation operates as an implicit fusion of ensemble techniques with knowledge transfer, thereby enhancing test accuracy through the combination mechanism.

author: Lawrence
title: Knowledge Transfer From Convolutional Pose Regression Models Through Targeted Compression
abstract: We introduce an approach for transferring knowledge from deep pose regressor networks toward constructing compact models suitable for Visual Odometry applications. Conventional distillation approaches depend on "dark knowledge" to facilitate effective transfer; however, since such knowledge cannot be extracted from pose regression tasks and educator outputs may lack reliability, we selectively apply knowledge transfer under conditions where educator confidence is high. We accomplish this via a confidence mechanism derived from educator cost, which assigns differential weighting to educator outputs during optimization. Integration of this confidence mechanism occurs through two complementary training strategies: Attentive Imitation Loss for the primary training objective, and Attentive Hint Training for acquiring intermediate representations from the educator. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural successful application of knowledge distillation to deep pose regression architectures. Experimental validation on KITTI and Malaga datasets demonstrates that student networks achieve comparable performance to educators while reducing parameters by as much as 92.95% and accelerating inference by 2.12x relative speed.

author: Pacheco
title: Decision Boundary-Aligned Knowledge Transfer via Adversarially-Discovered Supporting Points
abstract: Knowledge distillation remains an open challenge despite numerous recent approaches to facilitating learning in student networks through trained teacher models. This work offers a new framework centered on decision boundaries, a critical element characterizing classifier behavior. Since classifier generalization correlates strongly with decision boundary quality, and effective classifiers develop effective boundaries, transferring boundary-related information represents a promising distillation avenue. We employ adversarial attacks to identify samples that reinforce the decision boundary. Using this approach, the proposed method optimizes student network training through such boundary-supporting samples to convey more precise decision boundary information. Our experiments demonstrate that this technique achieves state-of-the-art performance and advances the field of knowledge distillation.

author: Smith
title: Quantifying Knowledge to Interpret the Mechanisms of Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We introduce an approach to elucidate why knowledge distillation succeeds by measuring and examining both task-aligned and task-unaligned visual concepts embedded within intermediate layers of deep neural networks. We formulate three specific claims as follows. 1. Through knowledge distillation, networks acquire a broader set of visual concepts compared to training from unprocessed data. 2. Knowledge distillation causes networks to acquire multiple visual concepts in parallel, whereas networks trained on unprocessed data tend to acquire these concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation produces more consistent gradient directions relative to training from unprocessed data. To examine these claims, we introduce three distinct mathematical measures for assessing feature representations. Our experimental evaluation involved testing multiple deep neural networks, which corroborated all three proposed claims.

author: Shaffer
title: Curated Knowledge Distillation Approaches for Machine Translation Networks
abstract: Knowledge distillation represents a prominent technique in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) to improve performance through transfer of instructor model's knowledge across individual examples during training. State-of-the-art translation results are regularly achieved by NMT systems on standard benchmarks. Prior investigations have given limited attention to the variable consequences and interrelationships of the training examples that function as channels for knowledge transfer from the instructor. We introduce an analytical framework for systematically evaluating how distinct examples contribute differently to distillation outcomes via examination of alternative sample groupings. Extensive empirical investigation reveals that increased instructor knowledge does not uniformly produce superior distillation results; information from particular examples may degrade overall performance. We put forward two straightforward but efficient sample filtering mechanisms—operating at batch scope and dataset scope—to determine which examples should participate in distillation. Our methods are tested on WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English, two substantial translation benchmarks. Results demonstrate improvements of +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU respectively relative to the Transformer baseline with our proposed filtering strategies.

author: Wolfe
title: Efficient and Dependable Data-Absent Knowledge Distillation Through Synthetic Sample Regeneration
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) in scenarios where original training data is unavailable enables the transfer of learned representations from a more complex neural network (teacher) into a streamlined counterpart (student). Standard approaches rely on a test set during the transfer phase to track student performance against held-out examples, selecting the iteration with the best result. When such validation data cannot be accessed concurrently with distillation, identifying the optimal student model becomes impossible. A robust data-free KD approach must therefore ensure monotonic improvements in student accuracy and not require validation data. The core difficulty arises because the student suffers from knowledge loss when the distribution of artificially created training examples shifts. Addressing this through explicit storage and periodic retraining on generated samples raises memory consumption and introduces privacy risks. We propose capturing the distribution of previously generated synthetic samples using a generative model, specifically a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) equipped with a specially designed training goal for learning synthetic representations effectively. Via this generative pseudo replay mechanism, the student receives samples from the VAE for retraining, avoiding knowledge loss without retaining any samples in memory. Evaluations on image recognition tasks demonstrate that the approach maximizes the expected accuracy of the distilled model while avoiding the substantial storage requirements associated with sample-keeping baselines.

author: Peterson
title: Knowledge Distillation in Parallel-Decoding Machine Translation: An Empirical Analysis
abstract: Parallel-decoding machine translation (NAT) models generate complete output sequences simultaneously rather than sequentially, delivering marked improvements in inference speed relative to sequential approaches. Knowledge distillation, a technique leveraging outputs from an established sequential model to construct training corpora, represents standard practice for such systems, yet delivers consistent improvements in translation quality whose underlying mechanisms remain unexplained. This study employs targeted experimental analysis to elucidate the role of knowledge distillation in training parallel-decoding systems. Our results demonstrate that this technique simplifies dataset structure and enables parallel-decoding architectures to capture output variation more effectively. Analysis reveals strong associations between model capacity and the appropriate degree of distilled-data simplification required for optimal translation performance. Drawing on these observations, we introduce multiple techniques for adjusting dataset structure to enhance parallel-decoding translation quality. Our approach reaches leading performance among parallel-decoding variants and substantially narrows the performance difference with sequential baselines on the WMT14 En-De benchmark.

author: Moore
title: Attention-Driven Feature Matching for Knowledge Distillation with Guided Emphasis
abstract: A teacher network trained on data provides transferable knowledge that can guide training of a student network through knowledge distillation. Conventional approaches require practitioners to manually designate which intermediate features should be aligned between teacher and student, relying on predetermined correspondences. This manual designation frequently results in suboptimal connections that reduce the effectiveness of knowledge transfer. Prior work has attempted to mitigate this challenge, yet identifying optimal correspondences under real-world conditions remains difficult. We propose an effective and computationally efficient knowledge distillation approach that leverages all feature levels across the teacher network while eliminating manual designation of connections. Our method employs an attention-based meta-network to compute relative feature affinities and adjusts knowledge transfer strengths across all feasible feature pairs using these learned weights. The result is more efficient identification of valuable correspondences compared to earlier methods, yielding superior results across model compression and domain adaptation benchmarks. Detailed qualitative investigation and systematic ablation experiments demonstrate the mechanisms underlying improvements. Code implementing the approach is publicly accessible at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Dynamic Teacher Weighting via Reinforcement for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deployment of large pre-trained models in NLP presents significant challenges due to computational requirements and inference latency. Knowledge distillation, a model compression technique, enables transfer of capabilities from teacher models to smaller student models. When distillation incorporates multiple teachers, current approaches typically either fix teacher model weights throughout training or apply uniform weights across all teachers. This work identifies that student models benefit from variable weighting of teachers, motivated by training instance complexity and student capacity constraints. We propose a reinforcement-based framework that assigns instance-dependent weights to each teacher to optimize student performance. Comprehensive evaluations across NLP benchmarks demonstrate the viability and practical benefits of this dynamic weighting approach.

author: Rogers
title: Reliability-Weighted Ensembled Teacher Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation leverages supplementary supervision from teacher models to enhance student model optimization. Recent efforts seek to harness multiple diverse teachers rather than relying on a single instructor. Yet current approaches typically aggregate predictions across teachers through averaging or other unsupervised combination techniques, which risks degrading student performance when certain teachers produce predictions of inadequate quality. We introduce the proposed method, which selectively weights each teacher's per-sample predictions according to reliability scores derived from true labels, prioritizing predictions that approximate one-hot distributions with elevated importance. The approach further stabilizes knowledge transfer by incorporating intermediate layers. Comprehensive evaluation across multiple teacher-student architectural combinations demonstrates that the proposed method substantially exceeds the performance of existing state-of-the-art alternatives.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation at the Feature Map Level in Online Settings
abstract: Feature maps encode substantial information regarding pixel-level values and their spatial interdependencies. Existing approaches to online knowledge distillation, however, have focused exclusively on class logits. We introduce an online knowledge distillation approach that leverages adversarial training to transfer both class logits and feature map knowledge jointly. Multiple networks are trained concurrently using discriminators that classify whether feature map distributions originate from different networks. Each network possesses a corresponding discriminator that labels its own feature maps as genuine and treats other networks' representations as artificial. Networks are incentivized to deceive their paired discriminators, thereby acquiring the feature distributions of partner networks. We demonstrate superiority over conventional pixel-wise matching approaches including L1 distance and argue this framework is better aligned with online distillation requirements. Additionally, we introduce a cyclic training protocol for joint optimization of three or more networks. Across different architectures on image classification benchmarks, our approach yields marked gains in accuracy, particularly when combining asymmetrically-sized student and teacher networks.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Reducing Depth in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks with many layers have demonstrated considerable capability for processing graph-structured information. However, the excessive depth of such architectures creates obstacles for implementation on resource-constrained platforms like mobile or embedded devices. Knowledge distillation through teacher-student frameworks provides a promising avenue for compressing these over-stacked models, with measurement of divergence between the instructor and learner networks being the critical component. Yet fixed distance metrics may not suit the heterogeneity of graph topologies, and determining the appropriate distance metric remains challenging. This work introduces an adversarial framework for graph model compression—described here as the proposed method—which employs antagonistic training between a generator and discriminator to dynamically identify and reduce divergence. Drawing on the observation that strong node-to-node and node-to-class associations underlie deep GNN effectiveness, we employ a learnable discriminator to assess inherited knowledge from both node-centric and class-centric perspectives. The discriminator differentiates between what the teacher network captures and what the student learns, while the student GNN acts as a generator attempting to defeat the discriminator. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of adversarial training to knowledge distillation for graph neural networks. Empirical evaluation across node-level and graph-level categorization tasks reveals substantial gains in student network performance. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method effectively transmits knowledge from an intricate teacher architecture to a streamlined student architecture.

author: Munoz
title: Data-Free Learning Transfer via Knowledge Distillation Without Access to Original Samples
abstract: Knowledge distillation addresses training a compact model (Student) by leveraging a high-capacity source model (Teacher) while preserving most of its capabilities. Current methods either require access to the training dataset itself or draw upon metadata derived from it to guide Student learning. Yet direct access to a Teacher's training data proves infeasible in many scenarios—when datasets are prohibitively large, or when privacy and safety constraints apply (e.g., biometric or medical information). This work introduces an approach that trains the Student without any dataset or metadata. Rather than relying on original samples, we generate synthetic Data Impressions extracted from the complex Teacher architecture, employing these reconstructions as replacements for authentic training examples during the knowledge distillation process. We term this framework "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and show that it achieves comparable generalization outcomes to standard distillation methods that use genuine training data across several widely-used benchmarks.

author: Roman
title: Equitable Feature Transfer via Knowledge Distillation in Visual Tasks
abstract: The pursuit of algorithmic equity has emerged as a critical concern in computer vision applications, particularly those involving decisions about people. Current methods struggle to eliminate model bias, which leads to disparate predictions across demographic groups. This work introduces a distillation-based framework designed to attenuate algorithmic bias in visual recognition through feature transfer, specifically employing maximum mean discrepancy techniques for equitable knowledge distillation. Though distillation is standard practice for enhancing predictive accuracy, prior literature does not to our knowledge systematically explore fairness improvements through distillation mechanisms. We provide theoretical grounding connecting knowledge distillation and fairness objectives. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method substantially reduces bias targeting underrepresented populations while maintaining accuracy across both synthetic and authentic facial recognition benchmarks.

author: Blair
title: Examining Knowledge Transfer Among Behavioral Policies
abstract: In deep reinforcement learning, transferring learned behavior from one agent to another through distillation represents a fundamental technique that has demonstrated substantial benefits. Such transfers have enabled faster optimization and improved agent capabilities on challenging problems [26, 32, 5, 8]. However, despite its conceptual accessibility and widespread adoption, distillation encompasses numerous distinct implementations whose relatively minor technical differences can substantially impact both resulting performance and the underlying objective being optimized. We systematically investigate the complete design space of policy distillation, evaluating the theoretical rationales and practical advantages of competing formulations via both analytical and experimental approaches. Our findings identify three preferred distillation variants, each suitable for different task contexts. Most notably, a novel formulation incorporating expected entropy regularization enables faster convergence across diverse scenarios while maintaining theoretical convergence guarantees.

author: Herrera
title: Fine-grained Feature Imitation for Knowledge Distillation in Object Detection
abstract: Deploying computationally expensive CNN-based recognition systems on resource-constrained devices remains a significant bottleneck. Knowledge distillation offers a compelling solution by enabling small student architectures to learn from large teacher models and achieve stronger generalization. Nevertheless, existing distillation approaches predominantly address classification tasks and largely overlook the complexities inherent in object detection. We demonstrate that standard knowledge distillation applied to detection models yields only marginal improvements. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a method leveraging spatial discrepancies in feature activations for fine-grained student-teacher imitation. Our key observation is that detectors prioritize regions proximate to objects. Consequently, feature activation differences at anchor positions corresponding to nearby objects encode critical generalization patterns from the teacher. We develop a procedure to identify these positions and encourage student models to match teacher feature responses at such locations for improved results. Validation on a simplified anchor-based detector architecture demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach on the KITTI dataset, achieving up to 15% mAP gains for student models relative to baselines without imitation. Further experiments using Faster R-CNN across diverse settings and standard benchmarks including Pascal VOC and COCO show that imitation reduces the student-teacher performance gap by up to 74%. Implementation available at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Knowledge Distillation with Alignment Guidance for Machine Reading Comprehension
abstract: Reading comprehension models currently achieve notable results through ensemble methods, yet such approaches suffer from computational overhead and susceptibility to adversarial examples. This work addresses these challenges using knowledge distillation to compress ensemble knowledge into a lightweight student model. We show that standard knowledge distillation applied to span-based answer prediction substantially improves reading comprehension performance. Building on this, we introduce two enhanced techniques that simultaneously discourage predictions toward ambiguous candidate answers and incorporate alignment signals extracted from the ensemble teacher. Our experimental results demonstrate that the best distilled student achieves only 0.4% F1 degradation relative to the ensemble on the SQuAD test set, with 12x speedup at inference time. Remarkably, this student exceeds teacher performance on adversarial SQuAD variants and the NarrativeQA benchmark.

author: Gray
title: Compressing BERT via Iterative Component Substitution
abstract: We introduce a compression technique for BERT founded on iteratively replacing its components. The method partitions BERT into discrete components, each paired with a smaller equivalent. During training, original components are randomly swapped with their reduced-scale counterparts, with the substitutes learning to replicate the original components' outputs. The swap frequency escalates systematically as training progresses, fostering greater integration between original and lightweight variants. Unlike preceding knowledge distillation methods for BERT compression, this technique requires no supplementary loss objectives. On the GLUE benchmark, the method demonstrates superior performance relative to existing knowledge distillation approaches, offering an alternative direction for model size reduction.

author: Arnold
title: Examining the Mechanisms and Limitations of Distributional Learning Transfer
abstract: Training compact networks to replicate larger instructional models through distributional transfer represents a widespread methodology in deep learning. This work demonstrates that while such transfer can enhance student model generalization performance, the mechanism differs substantially from conventional interpretations: substantial gaps frequently persist in the alignment of teacher and student predictive distributions, persisting even when the student possesses sufficient capacity for perfect replication. We identify optimization challenges as a fundamental barrier preventing the student from achieving teacher equivalence. Furthermore, we examine how distillation dataset characteristics influence the degree of distributional alignment achieved -- and demonstrate that improved alignment with the teacher does not invariably translate into enhanced student generalization capabilities.

author: Calderon
title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Generalization in Neural Vehicle Routing
abstract: Existing neural approaches to vehicle routing problems rely on identical distributions during both model development and evaluation (specifically, uniform distributions), creating difficulties when generalizing across different distributions. We address this limitation by introducing knowledge distillation into this domain and develop an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) framework intended to produce deep models with enhanced generalization capabilities. Our AMDKD scheme utilizes knowledge from several educators corresponding to representative distributions, enabling formation of a compact yet broadly-capable learner model. The framework incorporates an adaptive weighting mechanism enabling the learner to emphasize challenging distributions, thereby improving absorption of difficult-to-learn knowledge patterns. Experimental validation demonstrates that AMDKD matches or surpasses baseline neural approaches when evaluated on both held-out samples from the original distribution and new instances from shifted distributions, whether randomly created or sourced from established benchmarks (TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, AMDKD maintains broad applicability while requiring substantially fewer computational operations during deployment.

author: Montgomery
title: Detecting 3D Objects in Point Clouds via Graph Neural Message Passing
abstract: Standard 3D object detection frameworks demand intricate procedural sequences during both training and inference, necessitating extensive familiarization with particular benchmark characteristics. Taking motivation from recent approaches that eliminate non-maximum suppression in 2D detection, we introduce a detection architecture for point cloud data. Our approach formulates 3D detection as information passing across dynamically constructed graphs, extending the DGCNN paradigm toward predicting multiple object instances. This construction eliminates reliance on confidence-based aggregation or suppression post-processing steps. To address detection challenges in sparsely sampled point clouds, we present a specialized set-to-set knowledge transfer scheme. This strategy matches outputs between teacher and student networks while preserving invariance to permutation, substantially reducing the complexity of applying distillation to 3D detection. Experiments demonstrate superior results across driving scene benchmarks. Comprehensive examination of the detection architecture and knowledge transfer methodology is included.

author: Hensley
title: Improving Quantized Network Performance Through Teacher-Student Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Contemporary deep neural networks achieve outstanding performance across computer vision tasks including classification and detection, yet their substantial architectural complexity creates practical obstacles for resource-limited deployment scenarios. Such models demand considerable computational power and memory bandwidth, motivating investigation of reduction strategies. Two complementary approaches—quantization to reduced bit-widths and knowledge distillation from larger to smaller models—have emerged as viable solutions for constraining inference costs and memory usage. This work examines their synergistic application, demonstrating substantial accuracy gains when quantized networks leverage teacher-student knowledge transfer mechanisms. The proposed method achieves competitive results on ImageNet using ternary and 4-bit quantized ResNet variants. We outline three distinct strategies for integrating knowledge distillation across different phases of the training and operational workflow.

author: Ray
title: Using Knowledge Distillation to Convey Structural Prior Assumptions Across Neural Networks
abstract: When computational resources are scarce, datasets are limited, or test conditions diverge from training data distributions, the correct structural assumptions built into a model's architecture become vital. Yet identifying and implementing these architectural assumptions—and adapting them efficiently—often proves challenging. This work investigates knowledge distillation as a mechanism for transferring structural assumptions from one architecture to another. We examine pairs of architecturally distinct model families—LSTMs compared to Transformers, and CNNs relative to MLPs—across applications where architectural assumptions significantly influence performance. Our analysis characterizes how structural assumptions shape the solutions models settle into and examines whether and how thoroughly knowledge distillation enables such assumptions to transfer. We evaluate this transfer across multiple dimensions: downstream performance metrics alongside various properties of the final converged models.

author: Bush
title: Knowledge Distillation for Multi-Label Image Classification Using Weakly-Supervised Detection
abstract: Classifying multiple labels per image remains a demanding challenge in visual recognition tasks. Prior work has demonstrated that spatial region information (particularly features extracted from regions of interest) enhances multi-label classification performance. However, such approaches typically demand extensive annotations at the object level, including both class identifiers and spatial coordinates, which burdens the learning of object-specific visual representations. This work introduces an effective framework that leverages knowledge distillation from weakly-supervised detection to strengthen multi-label classification while requiring only image-level labels and avoiding bounding box supervision. The approach consists of two components: (1) training a weakly-supervised detection model using image-level supervision, then (2) integrating this model as a teacher into an end-to-end classification pipeline through a distillation module. The distillation mechanism transfers guidance at two levels: class-level predictions across the full image and object-specific feature representations from candidate regions. The student model receives this dual supervision while the teacher remains active only during training and can be removed at inference time, preserving computational efficiency. Validation across two major benchmarks (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) demonstrates that the framework outperforms existing approaches in both accuracy and computational cost.

author: Williams
title: Relational Distillation for Link Prediction Without Graph Traversal
abstract: Link prediction represents a core task where Graph Neural Networks have achieved strong empirical results. However, their practical utility is hindered by substantial inference time overhead stemming from complex graph neighborhood dependencies. Standalone MLPs offer computational efficiency but suffer from diminished predictive capacity due to insufficient relational information. This paper investigates knowledge distillation techniques to leverage the complementary strengths of both model classes for link prediction tasks. We first examine standard distillation variants, including matching predicted logits and aligning node representations. Finding these conventional approaches inadequate, we introduce a relational distillation framework designed to transfer relational knowledge centered on anchor nodes to student MLPs for link prediction. The framework incorporates rank-based matching and distribution-based matching mechanisms that provide complementary benefits. Our experimental evaluation shows that this approach substantially improves MLP-based link prediction, achieving superior performance to teacher GNNs on 7 of 8 tested benchmarks. Furthermore, a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference is attained on the large-scale OGB dataset relative to GNN-based approaches.

author: Perez
title: Adaptation via Distillation and Tuning from Black-box Classifiers in Single or Ensemble Settings
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to leverage labeled data from source domains to enable learning on target domains without annotation. Existing approaches typically demand access to raw source samples and employ data-dependent alignment techniques for transductive adaptation to target instances, potentially creating privacy risks for source data owners. While some recent work leverages white-box models from source domains, this remains vulnerable to data leakage via generative adversarial learning. We examine a practical UDA scenario where only black-box source models providing network predictions are accessible during target domain adaptation. We propose a framework comprising two stages: knowledge transfer from the source predictor through distillation to an architecture tailored for the target domain, followed by model refinement to enhance target domain fit. A key advantage is architectural flexibility—source and target networks need not share the same structure, enabling deployment even on resource-constrained systems. Evaluation across three adaptation regimes (single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) demonstrates that the approach achieves performance comparable to leading data-dependent methods. Implementation details are publicly released.

author: Roberts
title: Making Deep Neural Networks More Interpretable via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Across numerous domains—from speech processing and visual understanding to language modeling—Deep Neural Networks demonstrate remarkable performance. Yet in practice, particularly for ethically sensitive or safety-critical systems, mere predictive accuracy falls short of requirements; explainability becomes essential. The inherent opacity of Deep Neural Networks complicates the analysis and justification of their outputs, impeding broader applicability. We address this challenge by employing knowledge distillation to transfer complex neural networks into decision trees, thereby achieving both strong accuracy and transparency. Formulating this as a multi-output regression task, our empirical evaluation shows that the student model attains substantially higher accuracy (approximately 1% to 5% improvement) relative to standard decision trees when maintaining equivalent tree depth. Our implementation leverages TensorFlow to ensure feasibility with large-scale datasets. To our knowledge, this work represents the initial successful distillation of Deep Neural Networks into standard decision trees on multi-class classification problems.

author: Miller
title: Analyzing BERT Ranking Models via Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Pre-trained language models including BERT, trained on extensive textual datasets, have substantially improved modern information retrieval ranking architectures. Such models possess internal representations enabling detection of nuanced semantic correspondences between queries and passages. Yet the substantial computational requirements at prediction time present obstacles to practical deployment in large-scale search systems. This work investigates whether and in what manner search-relevant knowledge encoded in BERT can be conveyed to a compact ranker via distillation. Our findings show that employing an appropriate distillation strategy is essential, yielding up to nine times improvement in inference speed without sacrificing state-of-the-art ranking quality.

author: Hall
title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer in Federated Learning Systems with Heterogeneous Resource-Constrained Devices
abstract: Collaborative training across geographically dispersed devices enables construction of shared prediction models while keeping local data on-device, a paradigm known as federated learning. Current approaches typically impose uniform architectural and computational requirements on participating devices during local training, creating barriers for devices with limited resources. With device heterogeneity now prevalent, this work introduces a federated learning framework accommodating heterogeneous on-device models through zero-shot knowledge transfer. The method permits each device to select its on-device model independently based on available computational capacity. To facilitate knowledge transfer among structurally diverse on-device models, we employ zero-shot distillation that operates without requiring access to private on-device data, distinguishing our approach from prior work relying on publicly available data or pre-trained generative models. The computationally demanding distillation procedure runs on central infrastructure, enabling resource-constrained devices to participate fully. Within this distillation process, a generator undergoes adversarial optimization using an ensemble of models collected from participating devices. The resulting central knowledge transfers via on-device model parameters tuned for direct device-side integration. Empirical validation across multiple scenarios—including cases where device data distributions diverge, devices fail intermittently, on-device models vary architecturally, and devices lack knowledge of training objectives—confirms both effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.

author: Garcia
title: Reducing Size of Multimodal Vision-Language Models Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While vision-language (VL) pre-training has advanced significantly, developing compact VL architectures remains underexplored. This work applies knowledge distillation (KD) to downsize transformer-based VL models from large to compact scales. A principal obstacle involves the extraction of inconsistent region-based visual tokens across Student and Teacher object detectors, causing misalignment in intermediate layer representations and attention mechanisms. We address this by retraining the Teacher with region proposals originating from the Student detector, while retaining features from the Teacher's detector. Given such aligned inputs, the Teacher can effectively transmit knowledge via intermediate representations. We employ mean square error loss for matching attention patterns in transformer blocks and introduce a token-level noise contrastive objective that aligns hidden states against negatives retrieved from a memory queue. Results demonstrate substantial gains: the distilled compact VL models achieve 120.8 CIDEr on COCO image captioning (5.1 improvement versus undistilled baseline) and 69.8 accuracy on VQA 2.0 (0.8 higher than baseline). Comprehensive ablations at both pre-training and downstream fine-tuning phases validate the approach's effectiveness.

author: Ramirez
title: Adaptive Target Refinement through Recursive Self-Distillation
abstract: Deep neural networks benefit from numerous regularization approaches, including function space constraints, stochastic perturbations, input transformation, and related techniques that enhance their ability to generalize. We introduce a regularization strategy that iteratively applies self-distillation to soften one-hot label assignments via recursive incorporation of model predictions, thereby allowing the model to function simultaneously as both student and teacher. In this framework, target labels are continuously modified by blending gold-standard annotations with preceding outputs from the same model. This approach achieves an implicit hard example mining mechanism, as it rescales the gradient signal proportionally to classification difficulty. The method extends to any classification problem using discrete targets and readily integrates with existing regularization schemes for cumulative performance gains. Experimental evidence demonstrates improvements in both accuracy and calibration quality, including confidence ranking properties. Validation across three distinct applications—visual recognition, bounding box regression, and sequence-to-sequence translation—confirms consistent enhancements relative to established competitive approaches. Implementation details are accessible at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Low-Cost Convolutions via Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Deploying state-of-the-art deep networks on resource-constrained hardware remains challenging, yet systematic investigation of memory-accuracy tradeoffs for model compression is limited. We introduce a structural approach to knowledge distillation aimed at reducing memory footprint through mechanistic transformation of the teacher into a student model, requiring neither architectural redesign nor hyperparameter modification. By leveraging attention transfer, we generate Pareto frontiers across four standard benchmarks for compressed residual networks, characterizing the efficiency-performance relationship. Findings demonstrate that significant memory reduction is achievable with minimal accuracy degradation, and verify that students trained via distillation outperform those trained end-to-end without a teacher network.

author: Diaz
title: Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers in Sequential Stages for Question Answering on the Web
abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models such as BERT and OpenAI GPT have achieved strong performance on question answering tasks. Yet their substantial parameter counts result in prohibitively slow inference, creating significant obstacles for deployment in production settings. Standard compression approaches tend to lose information, resulting in performance degradation relative to the original models. We address this limitation through a sequential dual-phase framework using knowledge distillation from multiple instructors for web Question Answering systems. In the initial phase, we establish a general Q&A distillation objective to initialize the student model. Subsequently, the initialized student undergoes task-specific training where multiple teacher models provide supervision on various benchmarks (Web Q&A, MNLI, SNLI, RTE from GLUE), which mitigates overfitting tendencies present in any single teacher and facilitates transfer of broader knowledge to the student. Results demonstrate that our approach substantially surpasses established baselines and matches performance of the original teacher models while delivering marked improvements in inference efficiency.

author: Wood
title: Data Augmentation Quality in Knowledge Distillation: A Statistical Analysis
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) represents a training methodology in which neural networks leverage an instructor network to inform learning in a student network. Prior investigations of KD have concentrated predominantly on optimizing the network output dimension, particularly through modifications to the KD loss function. The relationship between KD and data augmentation (DA), however, remains unexplored. This work investigates the following: Which DA methods (such as CutMix) demonstrate substantially superior performance when applied to KD settings? How can one characterize an effective DA strategy for KD? Through statistical analysis, we propose that effective DA should minimize the covariance associated with teacher-student cross-entropy loss. We propose a measurable quantity—the standard deviation of the instructor network's mean probability (T. stddev)—and provide empirical validation. In addition to this theoretical framework, we develop an entropy-driven DA technique called CutMixPick that builds upon CutMix to achieve further improvements. Empirical validation across multiple experiments confirms these findings and demonstrates substantial gains achievable through enhanced DA choices in knowledge distillation.

author: Clark
title: Distillation via Paired Encoder-Decoder Learning for High-Resolution Generalized Artistic Transfer
abstract: Generalized artistic transfer exploits learned representations from large pre-trained CNN architectures (e.g., VGG-19) but faces practical limitations when processing ultra-high-resolution imagery under memory constraints. We introduce a novel distillation technique grounded in leveraging the synergistic relationship between encoders and decoders—a previously underexplored form of knowledge applicable to artistic transfer networks. This collaborative framework enables significant convolutional filter reduction. To address feature dimensionality inconsistencies during distillation, we employ a linear embedding loss that guides student models toward adopting linear transformations of teacher features. We demonstrate applicability across multiple artistic transfer formulations (WCT and AdaIN) with models compressed by factors up to 15.5 times. Notably, the compressed WCT variant enables ultra-high-resolution artistic transfer exceeding 40 megapixels on a 12GB GPU, marking an important capability milestone. Supplementary validation on optimization-driven stylization demonstrates algorithmic robustness across distinct methodological paradigms. Implementation details and model weights are provided at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Examining Common Training Procedures in Neural Networks: Warmup, Periodic Learning Rate Adjustments, and Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Standard neural network models have greatly improved in convergence velocity and ultimate results through various training procedures including knowledge transfer, learning rate scheduling, skip connections, and batch normalization. Without established theoretical foundations, systematic investigations examining these techniques can improve comprehension of neural network behavior and how models learn over time. Prior empirical work has employed linear path tracing and lower-dimensional projections for analysis, but both have substantial drawbacks. We instead analyze these techniques by adopting recently introduced methods for understanding loss surfaces and learned representations, specifically mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and propose explanations for why these procedures work effectively. We particularly investigate knowledge transfer alongside learning rate strategies involving periodic restarts and initialization phases, employing mode connectivity and CCA. The results of our empirical work indicate: (a) the commonly stated rationales behind periodic cosine adjustment schedules lack experimental confirmation; (b) that initialization phases at the training start function to suppress instability in later network blocks; and (c) that information transferred from the teacher model predominantly reaches later network blocks.

author: Zuniga
title: Distributed training of large neural networks via concurrent knowledge sharing
abstract: Ensemble methods and knowledge transfer techniques offer potential gains in model performance across diverse architectures but introduce practical hurdles: ensembles incur elevated inference costs while knowledge transfer demands intricate training procedures with numerous tuning decisions. We investigate a variant of knowledge transfer designed for simplicity, requiring neither multistage orchestration nor extensive hyperparameter customization. We demonstrate that concurrent knowledge transfer permits substantially greater algorithmic parallelism, accelerating convergence by approximately a factor of two on very large-scale datasets. Notably, performance improvements persist beyond the saturation point where conventional synchronous or asynchronous gradient-based optimization ceases to benefit from added parallelism. Two independently trained networks operating on disjoint data partitions exchange learned representations by optimizing consistency between model predictions; these predictions derive from outdated network parameters that need infrequent synchronization. Additionally, we show that concurrent knowledge transfer provides an economical mechanism for substantially improving the reproducibility of a model's output predictions. Empirical validation employs three benchmark settings: the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and a recently constructed dataset for neural language modeling exceeding $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens sourced from the Common Crawl web archive.

author: Wong
title: Leveraging Complex Student-Teacher Learning Patterns via Gradient Regulation for Enhanced Cross-Domain Model Robustness
abstract: Convolutional neural networks face substantial generalization challenges when confronted with insufficient or unrepresentative training data, limiting their deployment across practical applications. We introduce a versatile training approach grounded in knowledge distillation that incorporates a gradient filter serving as an innovative regularization mechanism to address this problem. Our framework harnesses the intricate distillation signals transmitted from teacher models alongside the proposed gradient filter to simplify the learning of underlying input-output relationships, thereby strengthening cross-domain robustness. Through comprehensive empirical evaluation across image classification, semantic segmentation, and reinforcement learning tasks, we demonstrate that the proposed technique substantially outperforms contemporary domain generalization methods. Furthermore, we employ two distinct evaluation metrics to examine the proposed approach, providing insights into the mechanisms through which knowledge distillation with gradient-based regularization enhances neural network generalization across diverse domains.

author: Lynch
title: Label Smoothing Regularization and Knowledge Distillation: Reexamining Connections
abstract: The process of knowledge distillation (KD) transfers learned representations from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Conventional understanding attributes such transfers to comparative knowledge among class relationships embedded in teacher outputs; consequently, only capable teachers have been used to improve less capable students. Through empirical investigation, we demonstrate unexpected phenomena: 1) the direction of KD can be reversed, enabling students to meaningfully enhance teachers; 2) teachers with notably worse accuracy than their students can nonetheless provide substantial gains. We develop theoretical explanations linking KD with label smoothing regularization, showing that 1) KD functions as an adaptive variant of label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization instantiates an implicit teacher-like entity for distillation. These insights suggest KD's effectiveness stems partly from regularization applied to probability distributions, a component as significant as or more so than inter-class relationship knowledge. Motivated by this perspective, we introduce a Student-Self Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) approach in which models are trained using self-supervision or hand-crafted regularization distributions without requiring an external teacher. This framework yields results matching those from standard KD with high-quality teachers, proving useful when superior teacher models are inaccessible. Tf-KD generalizes readily across neural network training scenarios. On ImageNet, Tf-KD delivers gains of up to 0.65% relative to strong reference implementations without requiring supplementary computation, outperforming improvements from label smoothing regularization alone.

author: Jackson
title: Collaborative Ensemble Learning Through Contrastive Feature Alignment for Image Understanding Tasks
abstract: We propose a framework for training multiple student networks jointly without a teacher, where networks exchange contrastive representations of learned embeddings. Conventional teacher-free knowledge distillation emphasizes output distributions but overlooks the richness of intermediate learned representations. Our approach operates by enabling networks to simultaneously share and absorb contrastive information across their architecture, thereby increasing the mutual information bound between model pairs. By propagating contrastive signals through multiple depths rather than restricting focus to final outputs, we introduce an adaptive mechanism that matches intermediate layers via meta-learning. This layer-wise extension consistently outperforms existing ensemble distillation strategies, as demonstrated across image classification benchmarks and downstream visual tasks. The improvements highlight how distributing contrastive learning across architectural depths produces superior feature learning. Empirical results validate that networks optimized through this stratified mutual interaction develop more discriminative representations. Implementation details are open-sourced.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Distillation Without Real Data
abstract: Knowledge distillation has shown significant development in recent times and emerged as a dominant approach for model compression and transferring learned knowledge. Yet nearly all contemporary KD methods depend on data, specifically requiring substantial quantities of authentic training examples or surrogate datasets that are typically inaccessible in practical applications. This work addresses this limitation and introduces an approach using adversarial distillation to produce a lightweight student architecture while operating without access to genuine data. A model discrepancy metric is proposed to quantify divergence between student and teacher architectures alongside an optimizable upper bound. The student and teacher models together operate as a discriminator working to minimize this divergence, whereas a generator produces adversarially challenging samples to maximize it. Empirical evaluation shows the proposed data-free technique achieves results on par with existing data-dependent approaches. Notably, the technique extends to semantic segmentation, a task substantially more demanding than classification, reaching optimal performance levels on this problem. Implementation details and trained weights are publicly accessible.

author: Martin
title: Transferring BERT Representations to Sequence-to-Sequence Speech Recognition via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Sequence-to-sequence models based on attention mechanisms have shown strong performance for automatic speech recognition, yet their unidirectional left-to-right decoding prevents them from exploiting right context. We employ knowledge distillation to integrate BERT, which accesses both leftward and rightward context, as an external language model into seq2seq ASR. Under this approach, BERT produces soft labels that supervise seq2seq ASR training. Additionally, we supply BERT with context spanning beyond individual utterances. Results on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese demonstrate substantial gains over the seq2seq baseline. Distillation from BERT surpasses distillation from a transformer language model restricted to leftward context alone. We additionally demonstrate that incorporating cross-utterance context yields benefits. Compared to alternative language model integration techniques including n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, our approach achieves superior performance without introducing additional computational requirements during inference.

author: Gray
title: Enhanced Feature Distillation through Ensemble Projection
abstract: Within knowledge distillation frameworks, prior work on transferring features has emphasized loss function design and layer selection, whereas the role of projection mechanisms connecting student to teacher architectures has received limited examination. This work first presents theoretical reasoning and empirical support for projection mechanisms, then introduces a projector ensemble strategy for enhanced distillation performance. We demonstrate that student architectures gain advantages from projection even when student and teacher feature spaces possess identical dimensionality. Without such a projection component, student network training constitutes simultaneous pursuit of two objectives: acquiring discriminative representations for the primary task and aligning student features with teacher features for knowledge transfer purposes. We hypothesize and experimentally confirm that lacking a projection module, students overfit to teacher feature distributions despite architectural and initialization differences. Such overfitting compromises the representational quality of deeper student features subsequently applied during classification. By introducing projection, the two objectives become separated; students concentrate more effectively on primary representation learning while maintaining ability to leverage teacher guidance via the projection mechanism. Leveraging this finding, we propose combining multiple projectors into an ensemble structure to boost student feature quality. Validation across datasets using various teacher-student configurations demonstrates efficacy of this approach.

author: Mayo
title: Understanding Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation: Examining Bias and Variance Interactions
abstract: Using a pre-trained network or combination of networks as a teacher provides guidance for training a student network through knowledge distillation. The teacher's outputs function as soft labels to supervise the student's training process. Previous work demonstrated that soft label-based supervision provides beneficial regularization effects on the student network. Yet from a statistical learning perspective, while regularization typically decreases variance, the joint behavior of bias and variance when employing soft labels remains unclear. This work examines how soft label distillation affects the bias-variance tradeoff. Our analysis reveals that this tradeoff operates differently for individual samples during the training process. Under fixed distillation temperature, we find a negative relationship between performance and the frequency of certain samples—termed regularization samples—which increase bias while decreasing variance. However, we also find empirically that entirely removing such samples harms distillation outcomes. Based on these findings, we introduce weighted soft labels that enable networks to manage the per-sample bias-variance tradeoff in an adaptive manner. Standard benchmark evaluation demonstrates the utility of this approach. Implementation is provided publicly.

author: Bowman
title: Compact Speech Models via Knowledge Distillation for Paralinguistic Tasks
abstract: Self-supervised methods have substantially enhanced speech representation quality in recent years. Yet deploying advanced embedding systems on edge devices remains challenging, constrained by scarce open implementations and considerable computational demands. This work tackles these constraints through the public distribution of compact paralinguistic speech models achieving near state-of-the-art results. Knowledge distillation forms the foundation of our approach, utilizing exclusively open datasets for model compression. We investigate multiple model architectures and conduct comprehensive benchmarking using the Non-Semantic Speech benchmark. Our larger compressed variant measures 314MB (a reduction to under 15% relative to the original 2.2GB teacher), matches the teacher's accuracy above 96% across 6 out of 7 evaluation tasks, and requires merely 6.5% of the training corpus. The minimal variant occupies just 22MB (1% of original scale) while surpassing 90% teacher accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Compared to the publicly available Wav2Vec 2.0 baseline, our models demonstrate superior performance on 6 of 7 benchmarks. Notably, our smallest variant beats Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion classification tasks while maintaining only 7% of its size.

author: Hawkins
title: Accelerated Distillation Approach for Image Analysis Tasks
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) proves valuable across image classification and self-supervised representation learning, yet computational inefficiency undermines practical utility. The principal bottleneck stems from repeated forward passes through large teacher networks, incurring substantial costs. ReLabel addresses this by generating a complete label map for each image; during training, region-specific labels are extracted via RoI alignment on this precomputed map, avoiding frequent teacher queries. Nonetheless, since these KD teachers derive from standard multi-crop procedures, inconsistencies emerge between the global label-map and localized labels, degrading results. We introduce the proposed method, which reproduces the distillation training stage to generate soft labels through multi-crop KD while surpassing ReLabel in speed by eliminating post-processing steps like RoI align and softmax computation. When processing multiple crops from a single image in one batch, our approach becomes faster than conventional classification pipelines.
