Experiments on ImageNet-1K with ResNet-50 achieve 79.8% accuracy, exceeding ReLabel by ~1.0% with improved speed. Self-supervised learning tasks similarly demonstrate computational gains. Implementation and pretrained models are publicly released.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-Weighted Fusion of Intermediate Layers for Teacher-Student Knowledge Distillation
abstract: During training, knowledge distillation couples a larger teacher network with a smaller student network to enable compression while maintaining performance quality. While distillation traditionally targets only final prediction outputs, intermediate layer representations offer additional supervision signals. This work addresses distillation at internal network depths. A fundamental challenge arises when teacher and student architectures lack direct layer correspondence, causing prior methods to discard certain teacher layers and only transfer knowledge from a limited selection. We propose an attention-based combinatorial mechanism to overcome this limitation. The approach learns to weight and merge information across multiple teacher layers, accounting for each layer's relative importance, before transferring the fused representations to student layers. We demonstrate this technique by compressing a 12-layer BERT into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer variants and evaluating them on the GLUE benchmark. Results indicate that the proposed attention-weighted fusion method achieves superior performance compared to existing distillation approaches.

author: Cameron
title: Exposure to Extensive Training Improves Smaller Model Performance: Pre-training's Role in Compact Architectures
abstract: Contemporary advances in language representation rely on computationally intensive models trained on large unlabeled corpora using self-supervised approaches. The deployment overhead of these models on specific tasks has motivated multiple compression strategies applied to pre-trained representations (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). Nonetheless, a straightforward approach—namely, conducting pre-training followed by task adaptation on smaller models—has received limited attention. We demonstrate that pre-training retains significance when applied to reduced-scale architectures, and that direct pre-training coupled with fine-tuning of compact models achieves performance comparable to more sophisticated concurrent techniques. Building upon pre-trained compact models, we investigate transferring task-specific information from large fine-tuned counterparts via conventional knowledge distillation. Our resulting straightforward yet powerful and broadly applicable strategy, termed Pre-trained Distillation, yields additional gains. Via comprehensive evaluation, we examine how pre-training and distillation interact across two previously under-explored dimensions: architectural scale and characteristics of unannotated task datasets. A striking finding emerges: these factors produce multiplicative benefits even when deployed sequentially using identical data. To facilitate subsequent investigations, we will release 24 pre-trained miniscule BERT variants in the public domain.

author: Parsons
title: Staged Difficulty Training for Knowledge Transfer in Dense Retrieval
abstract: Distilling knowledge from a ranking teacher into dense retrieval students has emerged as an approach to enhance model performance. We introduce a framework grounded in curriculum learning, termed the proposed method, which modulates the training difficulty by selectively varying the examples sourced from a re-ranking teacher model. The proposed method incrementally escalates training data complexity, thereby advancing the student model's optimization trajectory. Training commences with coarse-level preference judgments between document pairs according to the teacher's ranking, then transitions toward fine-grained relative ordering constraints. We instantiate a straightforward variant of the proposed method to strengthen two established dense retrieval architectures. Validation across three standard passage retrieval benchmarks confirms the framework's utility.

author: Perez
title: Resurrected Task Networks: Leveraging Single-Task Guidance for Enhanced Multi-Task Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Training multi-task neural networks to achieve competitive or superior performance relative to isolated single-task models remains difficult. We address this challenge by employing knowledge distillation, wherein specialized single-task models guide the learning of a unified multi-task architecture. This training procedure is augmented through annealing of instructors, an approach that smoothly shifts from reliance on distilled knowledge toward conventional supervised optimization, enabling the unified model to ultimately exceed the capabilities of individual teacher models. Empirical validation employs multi-task fine-tuning of BERT against the GLUE benchmark. Experimental findings demonstrate consistent gains in performance compared to both conventional single-task and conventional multi-task baselines.

author: Stewart
title: Differential Privacy in Neural Network Compression through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks on mobile devices requires addressing two critical challenges: the computational burden of large models exceeds device capacity, and building such models demands sensitive user data, raising privacy concerns. We introduce a private model compression framework that employs knowledge distillation with three complementary training objectives: hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to produce smaller, faster networks. Sensitivity is controlled through adaptive bounding and perturbation of knowledge transferred from the teacher model, satisfying differential privacy requirements. Additionally, we develop a sample selection strategy for queries that minimizes both the number of requests and cumulative privacy loss. Validation on Android devices and empirical testing demonstrate effective model reduction alongside robust privacy protection. Specifically, on SVHN with meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy, the proposed method achieves 20$\times$ compression, 19$\times$ acceleration, and 0.97% accuracy degradation.

author: Adams
title: Do Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation Genuinely Conflict: An Experimental Investigation
abstract: Recent claims have suggested that knowledge distillation and label smoothing are fundamentally at odds. This empirical study investigates whether such incompatibility truly holds across diverse settings. We first examine the claimed mechanism: that label smoothing diminishes relative distinctions within teacher logits. Subsequently, we establish connections between how label smoothing reshapes class distributions for semantically proximate versus distant pairs. A quantitative measure is introduced for assessing information loss in representations of individual samples. Through extensive visualizations, comprehensive tests, and detailed analysis, we then evaluate both limitations and overgeneralizations in the incompatibility thesis, conducting evaluations across Neural Machine Translation, Binary Networks, and Image Classification. Lastly, we delineate specific scenarios where label smoothing demonstrates diminished utility. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: Knowledge Distillation for Architecture-Independent Collaborative Learning Across Distributed Data
abstract: Can one construct a universal interface enabling arbitrary coalitions of data-possessing participants to engage in collaborative learning without commitment to particular architectures, and without access to curated representative datasets? Knowledge distillation represents a natural mechanism for developing such frameworks. Yet empirical investigation reveals that straightforward KD-based collaborative protocols exhibit substantial performance degradation. To understand this phenomenon, we introduce a theoretical analysis grounded in Federated Kernel ridge regression, capable of addressing both structural variation among models and heterogeneity in data distributions. Our results indicate that performance losses stem fundamentally from intrinsic constraints of knowledge distillation when operating under non-uniform data settings. We substantiate this framework through development of improved protocols leveraging KD and evaluate them experimentally with neural network implementations. While empirical outcomes remain limited, they align closely with theoretical predictions.

author: Hahn
title: Correlation-Based Distillation: A Universal Approach for Training Object Detectors Across Model Architectures
abstract: Knowledge distillation serves as a key training strategy for deploying efficient detection models. Limited prior work examines distillation scenarios involving architecturally distinct teacher and student networks. We empirically demonstrate that superior FPN features sourced from a heterogeneous instructor network provide benefits to the learner despite mismatched detection heads and assignment strategies. Naive feature alignment proves problematic in two respects. First, magnitude discrepancies across teacher and student representations can impose overly restrictive penalties on learning. Second, FPN stages and channels exhibiting high feature magnitude in the instructor network dominate loss gradients during distillation, suppressing contributions from remaining features and introducing spurious signal. We address these challenges through feature matching via Pearson Correlation Coefficient, which captures structural relationships while permitting magnitude flexibility. Experiments confirm consistent improvements over prior detection distillation approaches for both matched and mismatched student-teacher configurations. Training efficiency also increases. Leveraging a strong MaskRCNN-Swin instructor, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS attain 41.5% and 43.9% mAP respectively on COCO2017, representing gains of 4.1% and 4.8% relative to unguided counterparts.

author: Walter
title: Distillation Enhanced by Potent Instructors
abstract: Prior knowledge distillation approaches have operated under limited conditions, employing teacher architectures and training procedures that lack the sophistication of contemporary methods. This work introduces a technique for improved knowledge transfer when employing a more capable teacher network. Empirically, we observe that when the teacher is substantially stronger, the divergence in output distributions between pupil and instructor becomes markedly pronounced. Consequently, enforcing strict alignment through KL divergence-based objectives can hinder learning and cause conventional techniques to degrade. We demonstrate that maintaining the structural patterns among teacher and student outputs alone proves sufficient, and develop a similarity-based objective function to explicitly capture the fundamental inter-class ordering relationships inherent to the teacher's predictions. Furthermore, recognizing that individual examples exhibit varying degrees of semantic alignment with each category, we generalize this relational correspondence to encompass within-class comparisons as well. The proposed strategy is straightforward while remaining effective, with thorough evaluation confirming robust compatibility across different network topologies, parameter scales and optimization procedures, attaining competitive results across image recognition, object localization, and dense prediction benchmarks. Implementation is publicly accessible via: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Privacy Protection through Ensemble-Based Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation in Federated Learning
abstract: In federated learning environments, decentralized training data is used by distributed participants to collaboratively construct a unified model. Common FL approaches either exchange model parameters or apply co-distillation to mitigate issues stemming from non-uniform data distributions, though these techniques face limitations in communication costs and present significant privacy risks. We introduce a method combining privacy protection with reduced communication overhead for FL settings, leveraging single-pass offline knowledge distillation from public cross-domain unlabeled data. Our approach uses a quantized and noisy ensemble of fully-trained local model outputs to enhance privacy safeguards while maintaining performance levels. Comprehensive evaluations across image and text categorization demonstrate that our privacy-protecting strategy achieves stronger results than standard FL baselines in both performance and communication requirements.

author: Rios
title: Knowledge Distillation for Enhanced Neural Topic Modeling
abstract: Document collections frequently require extraction of interpretable semantic categories to facilitate human understanding. We employ knowledge distillation to synthesize strengths from both conventional probabilistic topic models and fine-tuned transformer architectures. Our flexible approach integrates with any neural topic model architecture to enhance topic quality, which we validate through two models with different structural designs, achieving competitive topic coherence scores. We demonstrate that our versatile framework yields performance gains not merely across the full topic inventory in aggregate form, as typically measured, but also when evaluating individual topics through direct paired comparisons.

author: Foster
title: Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers for Click-Through Rate Prediction
abstract: Deep neural networks have gained widespread adoption for click-through rate (CTR) prediction in industrial settings, delivering enhanced predictive performance across numerous applications. Contemporary approaches emphasize architectural complexity to capture nuanced feature interactions and temporal variations in user engagement patterns. Yet greater architectural sophistication introduces computational overhead that degrades inference speed and limits real-time deployment feasibility. We propose an alternative training methodology grounded in knowledge distillation (KD), wherein a teacher model conveys learned representations to a student model through a teacher-student learning framework. This distillation approach enables training of a baseline DNN student while obtaining improvements beyond performance demonstrated by leading teacher models. Building upon this foundation, we investigate whether employing an ensemble of multiple teachers can further enhance student model training quality. Additional contributions include teacher gating mechanisms and early termination strategies guided by distillation loss. Evaluation encompasses benchmarking against 12 baseline approaches using three large-scale industrial datasets, with validation through both offline metrics and online A/B tests, confirming the efficacy of the proposed distillation-based training paradigm.

author: Rocha
title: Cross Distillation for Few-Sample Network Compression
abstract: Reducing the size of deep neural networks has become commonplace for deploying efficient models. However, the majority of existing approaches depend on retraining using ample labeled data, which introduces potential privacy and security risks. In this work, we explore compression under severe data scarcity: when only a handful of examples per class are available, what techniques enable effective network reduction while maintaining performance? Few-sample compression presents a fundamental difficulty: the original network produces substantial inference errors that accumulate across sequential layers as the compressed variant tends to memorize the scarce training set. Such errors compound at each stage, degrading ultimate predictions. We introduce cross distillation, a novel strategy based on layer-wise knowledge transfer. By alternating teacher and student network components across intermediate representations, cumulative layer-to-layer errors become substantially attenuated. The framework integrates naturally with standard compression procedures including weight pruning. Results across multiple datasets show that cross distillation yields substantial gains in student network performance when training examples remain limited.

author: Ellis
title: Leveraging Global Topology in Representation Distillation for Efficient Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Deploying lightweight graph neural networks with knowledge transfer from larger, more sophisticated teacher models enables resource efficiency. Prior distillation approaches for GNNs introduced the Local Structure Preserving loss, which enforces alignment of edge-based local structural attributes in node embeddings between teacher and student architectures. This study investigates whether maintaining the overarching topological structure of the teacher's graph representations yields superior distillation outcomes for GNNs, given that real graphs frequently exhibit hidden correlations and spurious edges. We propose the proposed method, incorporating contrastive learning mechanisms to implicitly maintain global topology by bringing student node embeddings into correspondence with teacher embeddings within a unified feature space. We further develop an extensive evaluation suite across large-scale real-world graphs with meaningful divergence between teacher and student model performance. Results on 14 different GNN variants across 4 benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method consistently strengthens both performance and generalization in resource-constrained GNNs, surpassing the Local Structure Preserving approach (including its global variant) and techniques adapted from 2D vision domains. Investigation into representational alignment between teacher and student embedding spaces indicates that the proposed method achieves balance between local and global preservation, whereas topology-focused baselines excel at either one dimension or the other. Implementation details are disclosed for reproducibility.

author: Baker
title: Addressing Rare Word Rendering Through Joint Exploitation of Native and Synthetic Corpora in Sequence Prediction Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) systems typically rely on knowledge distillation (KD) to generate synthetic training corpora. A distributional mismatch emerges for rare tokens when comparing distilled against native datasets, resulting in degraded accuracy for rare token generation. We mitigate this issue by incorporating genuine data into NAT via pretraining strategies. Through examination of directional word alignments, KD produces deterministic pairings between infrequent source tokens and their targets yet inadequately captures alignments involving infrequent target tokens. We therefore introduce reverse KD to recover additional alignment structures corresponding to rare target tokens. Synthesizing both native and synthetically produced examples, we develop an integrated training protocol that leverages each data type's distinct advantages to enhance NAT outcomes. Evaluation across five translation corpora using two state-of-the-art model architectures demonstrates substantial and consistent gains, particularly in reducing misrenderings of rare tokens. Our method achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points respectively on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English benchmarks. Implementation, datasets, and model checkpoints are publicly released.

author: Wright
title: Semantic Knowledge Transfer for Unified Video Scene Analysis
abstract: Comprehensive perception of visual scenes is essential for autonomous systems. Prior research demonstrates that neural networks can infer geometric structure (depth) and motion (optical flow) from single-camera footage without requiring explicit ground truth supervision, a constraint that makes direct annotation impractical for these particular modalities. This work advances scene comprehension from monocular video by jointly modeling depth, motion, and semantic content, with the semantic signal supplied through a pre-trained teacher distilling synthetic reference frames. The approach tackles all three tasks concurrently via: (a) an innovative learning scheme incorporating knowledge distillation with unsupervised learning and (b) a streamlined architectural design supporting efficient inference across resource-intensive GPUs and resource-constrained edge devices. Our experiments validate the framework across the board and report state-of-the-art performance on monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and motion segmentation tasks.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation in Distributed Settings
abstract: Decentralized machine learning frequently avoids transmitting unprocessed information by having multiple agents communicate learned model states instead. Federated learning represents such a paradigm, wherein gradient or weight vectors transmit between participants. Yet when bandwidth is restricted, this communication pattern incurs prohibitive overhead, particularly given the vast parametric dimensions of contemporary deep models. An alternative emerges through federated distillation, which transmits only model predictions—typically far lower dimensional than the models themselves (for instance, 10 categories per image in MNIST). This work aims to clarify federated distillation fundamentals while establishing bandwidth advantages and breadth of applicability. To illuminate how federated distillation functions, the opening section provides novel asymptotic characterization of two core distillation variants—knowledge distillation and co-distillation—leveraging neural tangent kernel theory. Thereafter, a reference system for classification scenarios receives detailed treatment, with empirical comparison highlighting both classification quality and communication demands against conventional federated learning. Finally, to underscore relevance across diverse distributed scenarios, the concluding section explores two concrete instantiations: federated distillation over asymmetric wireless transmission channels and federated distillation applied to learning agent optimization.

author: Baker
title: Combining Diverse Models via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We address the challenge of consolidating knowledge across multiple classifiers possessing distinct architectures and output categories into a consolidated model, using only an unannotated generic dataset. The consolidation of heterogeneous classifiers presents practical utility in distributed-data scenarios where individual data sources are restricted from sharing their raw information—for instance, when privacy regulations apply—yet can contribute trained models. Furthermore, sources may have incomplete coverage of target classes owing to local data constraints, and may employ differing model architectures reflecting their computational limitations. We develop an extension of knowledge distillation designed to merge such heterogeneous classifiers. We establish a probabilistic correspondence linking classifier outputs to a unified class probability distribution. Drawing from this correspondence, we present two methodological families—one grounded in cross-entropy optimization and another leveraging matrix factorization—enabling prediction of class confidence values across the complete class space from unlabelled examples. These predicted confidences serve as surrogate targets for training a consolidated model. Results on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 demonstrate substantial improvements relative to basic distillation variants and attain performance approaching that of unified supervisedly-trained baselines.

author: Richards
title: Knowledge Distillation and Adversarial Networks for Text Synthesis
abstract: Text synthesis via generative adversarial networks (GANs) presents challenges distinct from computer vision applications, particularly due to text's inherently discrete structure. This work leverages knowledge distillation to enable effective application of GANs in natural language processing tasks including machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. We employ autoencoders (AEs) to generate continuous sentence representations—smooth distributions assigning non-zero probability across multiple words—and distill these representations to guide generator training toward producing analogous smooth outputs. Validation across multiple datasets demonstrates that the proposed method surpasses traditional unpretrained GAN-based text generation with respect to BLEU scores and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measurements.

author: Hurst
title: Efficient Recommendation Models Through Knowledge Transfer: Achieving High Accuracy in Compact Student Networks
abstract: We introduce a knowledge distillation approach adapted for learning to rank contexts, enabling the development of reduced-size models that maintain strong predictive capabilities in recommendation scenarios. This technique, termed ranking distillation, leverages a larger teacher model to guide a smaller student model through joint learning from both direct training signals and teacher supervision on document and item rankings. The resulting student model delivers ranking performance comparable to its larger teacher counterpart while requiring substantially less memory, thereby improving computational efficiency during deployment. The proposed framework exhibits flexibility across different architectural choices for both teacher and student ranking models, remaining agnostic to their specific implementations. We identify and address technical obstacles particular to applying distillation within ranking-based problems. Evaluation on benchmark datasets with contemporary recommendation approaches demonstrates that the method achieves its intended objectives: student models trained via this distillation strategy retain less than half the parameters of teacher models while preserving ranking accuracy equivalent to the teacher and substantially surpassing student models trained conventionally without distillation guidance.

author: Ross
title: Distillation from Multiple and Single Educators for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: A fundamental approach in knowledge distillation involves instructing a student architecture using guidance from a more capable educator network to achieve superior performance. Performing translation through a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) system incurs significant computational overhead; employing a compact variant reduces runtime substantially. This work illustrates methods to migrate the translation performance of both ensemble-based and oracle BLEU educators into a streamlined NMT architecture. Additionally, we report performance gains when the educator shares identical dimensions and structure with the student architecture. Since student model optimization remains computationally demanding, we propose a selective training procedure leveraging educator-derived signals that accelerates optimization while simultaneously improving translation performance. The methodology integrates seamlessly into existing infrastructure without architectural modifications and generalizes across diverse NMT frameworks to minimize inference latency.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing and Enhancing Vocabulary Selection Performance in Simultaneous Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models rely on knowledge distillation (KD) to simplify training data using an autoregressive teacher, yet we demonstrate empirically that this process transfers vocabulary selection mistakes from the teacher to the NAT model, particularly affecting infrequent terms. We propose mitigating this issue by incorporating raw data directly into NAT training, recovering information about low-frequency words that distillation discards. Specifically, we introduce a supplementary Kullback-Leibler divergence component based on contrasting the vocabulary selections between the NAT model and those present in unprocessed data. Validation across diverse language pairs and network configurations indicates broad applicability and consistent gains. Detailed investigation validates that improvements stem from diminishing vocabulary selection errors among rare words. Our method achieves 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English respectively, advancing state-of-the-art NAT benchmarks. Implementation will be made publicly available.

author: Bright
title: Efficient and Compact Lipreading via Knowledge Distillation for Real-World Deployment
abstract: Neural network advances have driven substantial improvements in lipreading. While recent studies have focused on optimizing performance through architecture design and enhancing generalization capabilities, a considerable gulf persists between research prototypes and systems suitable for actual deployment. This paper addresses this gap through three key contributions: (1) Self-distillation techniques elevate performance substantially on LRW and LRW-1000, reaching 88.5% and 46.6% respectively. (2) We introduce architectural innovations including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network head that substantially decreases computational requirements relative to the baseline (which was already relatively efficient). (3) We demonstrate that knowledge distillation effectively restores accuracy in reduced-capacity variants. The resulting model family spans multiple accuracy-computational cost tradeoffs. Notably, our best lightweight variants match contemporary state-of-the-art accuracy while achieving 8.2x and 3.9x reductions in computational expense and parameter count respectively, potentially enabling practical deployment of lipreading systems.

author: Hicks
title: Instructing Models for Domain Shift: A Distillation Framework
abstract: In practice, distribution mismatch between training and evaluation datasets presents a significant obstacle across numerous applications. Conventional Deep Learning methods addressing domain adaptation require simultaneous training across both source and target domains, limiting their utility when rapid model adjustment to multiple domains is needed or when domain characteristics shift over time, such as in dynamic spam filtering systems. We introduce a framework extending Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to address domain adaptation challenges. Our approach enables a student model to attain optimal performance in unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation on sentiment analysis tasks by leveraging domain-specific knowledge from multiple teachers alongside inter-domain relationships. For single-teacher scenarios, domain similarity alone proves insufficient for assessing reliability. Consequently, we introduce a straightforward measure demonstrating strong alignment with target domain performance. Incorporating high-confidence samples identified through this metric allows the student model to achieve optimal results in the single-source setting.

author: Williams
title: Adversarial Belief Matching for Knowledge Transfer Without Data
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a well-trained large network to a more compact network represents an important challenge in contemporary machine learning. The scarcity of training data and increasing constraints on data privacy make it difficult to access the original training corpus used to train the large network. We introduce an approach that trains a student network to align its outputs with those of the teacher network without requiring any actual data or associated metadata. This is accomplished by employing an adversarial generator to discover images where the student's predictions diverge most from the teacher, subsequently leveraging these images for student training. The resulting model demonstrates strong approximation of its teacher on elementary tasks such as SVHN, and reaches state-of-the-art results on CIFAR10 in the few-shot distillation regime (100 images per class), all without utilizing any original data. We additionally introduce a measurement for assessing alignment of beliefs around decision margins, revealing that our data-free student exhibits markedly superior correspondence with the teacher relative to students trained via conventional distillation with actual data. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: Knowledge Distillation from Graph Neural Networks: A Framework for Improved Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
abstract: Graph-based semi-supervised classification remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning. While recent advances in graph neural networks have demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional approaches like label propagation, the intricate design of these models introduces computational overhead and may obscure meaningful patterns already present in the data, particularly the tendency of neighboring nodes to share labels. This work introduces a distillation-based approach to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained GNN (teacher model) to a simpler student architecture. The student is constructed from two fundamental components: label propagation and feature transformation, which respectively encode structural and attribute-based inductive biases inherent to graph data. Specifically, the student comprises a learned combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation layers. By this design, the student simultaneously leverages both intrinsic priors within the graph and knowledge extracted from GNN teachers, yielding superior predictive performance. Additionally, the student model provides greater transparency in its decision-making process relative to standard GNNs. We evaluate the framework across five established benchmark datasets using seven teacher architectures, namely GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP. Results demonstrate consistent improvements of 1.4%-4.7% over the teacher models on average. Implementation details are provided at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

author: Burton
title: Hardware-Optimized Pruning via Block Structure for Scaling Down Large Transformer Language Models
abstract: Substantial pre-trained language models have shown strong empirical performance across numerous natural language processing (NLP) benchmarks. Yet the constraints on memory capacity and inference throughput in practical hardware settings have limited adoption of these models, particularly within resource-constrained edge environments. This paper introduces a method for constructing efficient transformer-based representations by applying block-structured pruning adapted for hardware deployment. We employ reweighted group Lasso as part of our optimization strategy within the block-structured framework. The resulting models exhibit substantially diminished parameter counts and reduced computational requirements alongside strong compression outcomes. Evaluation across multiple architectures—BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT—using the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) suite demonstrates compression of up to 5.0x while maintaining comparable or unchanged task performance. The approach complements compact variants created through knowledge distillation; when applied to DistilBERT, an additional 1.79x average compression factor becomes attainable without measurable performance loss. This technique permits effective model deployment in memory- and power-limited edge computing scenarios.

author: Conner
title: Transferring BERT-Learned Representations into Shallow Recurrent Architectures for Language Tasks
abstract: Recent trends in natural language processing have emphasized increasingly sophisticated and layered neural architectures, exemplified by advanced representation learners such as BERT, GPT, and ELMo. This momentum has fostered assumptions that older, simpler neural models for linguistic understanding lack contemporary competitiveness. We challenge this presumption by showing that basic, minimal-parameter networks remain viable when trained through knowledge distillation from BERT, without requiring architectural expansion, supplementary datasets, or novel input representations. We extract learned patterns from BERT into both standard single-layer BiLSTM models and siamese variants optimized for sentence-pair classification. Testing across paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment analysis benchmarks yields performance matching ELMo-based systems, while reducing parameter count by roughly 100-fold and cutting computational latency by approximately 15-fold.

author: Henderson
title: Distillation-Enhanced MLPs for Rapid Inference Without Graph Access
abstract: Graph Neural Networks remain dominant in graph-based learning tasks, delivering robust performance across node classification benchmarks. Industrial applications, however, frequently encounter bottlenecks due to computational constraints stemming from neighbor dependencies. GNN inference requires accessing nodes several hops away in the neighborhood structure, imposing substantial overhead on latency-sensitive systems. While techniques such as pruning and quantization reduce Multiplication-and-ACcumulation counts and accelerate GNNs, they do not adequately address the underlying graph dependency challenge. Multi-layer perceptrons, lacking any graph dependency, execute substantially faster during inference compared to GNNs; nevertheless, their predictive accuracy for node classification lags behind graph-based approaches. Building on these complementary limitations and advantages, this work combines GNNs with MLPs through knowledge distillation mechanisms. Results demonstrate that MLP performance can be substantially elevated through GNN-based distillation. The resulting models, termed graph-independent neural networks, bypass graph dependency entirely during inference. These models achieve competitive accuracy while providing 146X-273X faster inference than GNNs and 14X-27X faster inference than competing acceleration approaches. Across 7 datasets under production conditions encompassing both transductive and inductive scenarios, the proposed method achieves 12.36% average accuracy gain over baseline MLPs and demonstrates parity with GNNs on 6 out of 7 datasets. Empirical investigation clarifies the conditions under which competitive performance is attainable and identifies the approach as particularly suited for systems with strict latency constraints.

author: Brown
title: Integrated Compression for Image-based Transformers
abstract: Image-based transformers (ViTs) have increasingly gained adoption in recent times. Without relying on dedicated convolution-like operations, these models achieve strong results when trained adequately on large-scale datasets. Yet the computational demands remain burdensome, stemming from repeated multi-head self-attention blocks and associated components. While compressing convolutional models has been extensively studied with considerable achievements, Vision Transformer compression is nascent, with previous approaches addressing narrow subsets of the compression problem. We introduce an integrated framework for ViT compression combining three complementary approaches: channel/neuron removal, depth reduction through layer omission, and knowledge distillation. We establish a constraint-based joint optimization objective, simultaneously tuning network parameters, per-layer removal rates and patterns, and layer omission settings under a distillation objective. A primal-dual method resolves this optimization task. Testing across multiple ViT instantiations—including DeiT and T2T-ViT variants on ImageNet—demonstrates superior performance against established baselines. Notably, DeiT-Tiny reaches 50\% of baseline computational load with negligible accuracy degradation. Implementation details are publicly accessible.

author: James
title: Learning Stable Multimodal Features via Iterative Self-Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Vision-language models like CLIP struggle with the inherent noise in web-sourced image-text pairs due to their many-to-many associations, resulting in computational and data-efficiency limitations. We propose a framework grounded in cross-modal contrastive learning that leverages iterative self-distillation along with smooth image-text alignments to extract resilient representations despite noisy inputs. Rather than fixed targets, our model transfers its own learned representations to create dynamic soft-alignment objectives for randomly selected image-caption pairs within each batch, updating weights accordingly. Evaluation on 14 separate benchmarks demonstrates consistent improvements relative to CLIP across three distinct evaluation protocols: (a) zero-shot classification performance, (b) linear probe adaptation, and (c) image-text retrieval tasks, with no additional computational burden. Robustness evaluation using ImageNet-based diagnostic tools indicates our approach exhibits greater stability against natural domain shifts than both ImageNet baselines and CLIP. Furthermore, scaling experiments across pretraining datasets of different sizes spanning two orders of magnitude demonstrate that advantages over CLIP increase proportionally with training set size.

author: Ferrell
title: Enhanced Supernet Optimization via Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Neural architecture search with weight-sharing is a powerful method for automating the discovery of efficient network designs. In this approach, a supernet encompasses all candidate architectures as embedded sub-networks and undergoes joint training alongside these sub-networks. The effectiveness of such methods fundamentally depends on transferring knowledge from the supernet to its constituent sub-networks through distillation. Traditional distillation approaches using KL divergence can produce student sub-networks that either overestimate or underestimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, thereby compromising sub-network quality. We propose employing a more general alpha-divergence formulation to enhance supernet training. Through adaptive selection of the alpha parameter, we mitigate both overestimation and underestimation of teacher model uncertainty. The method extends to both slimmable networks and weight-sharing architecture search, yielding substantial empirical gains. Our resulting model family demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art alternatives including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS across various computational budgets. We attain 80.0% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 444M FLOPs. Implementation and trained weights are publicly released.

author: Rice
title: Distillation-Enhanced Sequential Representation for Improved Generalization in Synthetic Media Detection
abstract: Substantial progress in artificial intelligence has occurred, yet systems typically operate within fixed dataset assumptions in unchanging conditions. The study of continual learning investigates sequential adaptation from flowing information streams, mirroring how natural systems acquire knowledge. Deepfakes and computer-generated face imagery represent pressing challenges in multimedia. While existing detection approaches achieve strong performance metrics, limitations emerge when evaluation involves diverse settings beyond their training scope. This work addresses such gaps by incorporating sequential learning principles into network training, aiming to enhance efficiency across data processing. We introduce the proposed method combining continual learning, representation learning, and knowledge distillation mechanisms. The approach handles successive domain adjustment scenarios involving emerging deepfake and GAN-synthesized facial datasets, while suppressing catastrophic forgetting within teacher-student frameworks. Comprehensive empirical validation shows the method successfully adapts across multiple sources, achieving strong results on degraded deepfake footage and generator-based face images, and surpasses established comparison baselines.

author: Maddox
title: Compressing BERT via Flexible Intermediate Layer Alignment Using Earth Mover's Distance
abstract: Transformer-based pre-trained language models such as BERT deliver robust performance across numerous NLP applications, yet their substantial memory requirements and computational demands make deployment problematic on devices with limited capacity. We introduce a knowledge distillation approach for BERT compression employing flexible many-to-many layer alignment, wherein each intermediate student layer may draw knowledge from any intermediate teacher layers. This flexibility enables adaptive learning across diverse NLP tasks by leveraging varying linguistic representations encoded in BERT's intermediate layers. We employ Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to determine the optimal alignment cost for transferring knowledge from teacher to student network, enabling effective many-to-many layer matching across architectures of differing dimensions. Additionally, we develop a cost attention mechanism to automatically derive the layer weights incorporated in EMD computation, intended to enhance accuracy and reduce training duration. Evaluation on the GLUE benchmark demonstrates competitive results against established baselines with respect to both classification accuracy and compression ratio.

author: Valencia
title: Deep Learning Model Reduction Techniques for Natural Language Tasks: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial advances in natural language processing and information retrieval through architectures such as RNNs, GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformer-based systems including BERT, GPT-2, MT-DNN, XLNet, T5, T-NLG, and GShard. However, these models exhibit substantial parameter counts. Practical deployment scenarios necessitate models that occupy less memory, execute with minimal latency, and consume reduced computational resources. This survey examines six reduction strategies—Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer variants—enabling adaptation of large architectures for production NLP systems. Given mounting pressure to develop resource-efficient systems and the expanding literature addressing these concerns, we present this work to synthesize contributions from the community into an integrated framework.

author: Smith
title: Automated Search-Based Compression of Generative Adversarial Networks Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deploying Generative Adversarial Networks to resource-constrained environments like mobile devices has motivated research into generator compression, yet prior work addressing this problem typically applies only to particular architectures and loss functions. We leverage recent advances in AutoML-guided neural network compression by proposing a framework that automatically discovers compact generators under specified computational budgets. The discovery process employs an efficiently designed search space and is supervised through knowledge distillation from the original GAN. Our approach operates end-to-end without requiring trained discriminators and extends across diverse GAN variants. We conduct experiments on image translation and super resolution, demonstrating that the resulting models achieve substantial size reductions while maintaining or exceeding the performance of existing compression baselines. The method is fully automated and generally applicable to different GAN architectures despite varying loss objectives. Code and trained model weights are publicly released.

author: Le
title: Reconsidering Embeddings from Videos and Skeletal Data for Recognizing Everyday Activities
abstract: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) has motivated fusion approaches leveraging both RGB streams and 3D skeletal information. ADL recognition proves challenging due to visual and kinematic similarities across distinct actions, requiring capture of nuanced discriminative characteristics. Rigid 3D ConvNets struggle to encode subtle motion patterns effectively, prompting hybrid methods that fuse RGB with skeletal data. However, extracting 3D skeleton information from video carries substantial computational overhead without dedicated sensors, hindering deployment in latency-sensitive real-world scenarios. How can skeleton information be optimally leveraged for ADL classification? We address this through enhancing a skeleton-guided attention mechanism: the proposed method explores two complementary pathways. The first transfers skeletal knowledge to the RGB branch via feature-level distillation; the second reproduces skeleton-guided attention using attention-level distillation. Integration of both distillation pathways yields a unified architecture. Evaluation demonstrates competitive performance alongside computational efficiency gains and robustness against skeletal noise. The model achieves superior results relative to established baselines across 4 benchmark datasets, both with and without skeletal input. Implementation details and reproducible resources are provided.

author: Maldonado
title: Feature Imitation as a Knowledge Transfer Mechanism
abstract: Knowledge distillation represents a well-established approach for constructing compact neural networks (termed "student") by leveraging large-capacity neural networks (termed "teacher"). Conventional approaches employ the teacher's soft logits as additional training signal for the student network. We propose instead that directing the student to replicate the teacher's features at the penultimate layer constitutes a superior strategy. Mimicking features provides two advantages: students extract richer information directly from teacher representations, and the method functions even when teachers lack a softmax layer. Experimental results demonstrate performance surpassing conventional KD. To enhance feature mimicking further, we decompose features into magnitude and directional components. The teacher's contribution should grant flexibility regarding student feature magnitudes while encouraging focused attention on directional alignment. We introduce a loss function constructed using locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to achieve these goals. This loss mechanism improves directional mimicking precision, allows feature magnitudes greater flexibility, and attains optimal distillation results. Theoretical justification explains the role of LSH in supporting directional feature replication. Applications to multi-label recognition and detection tasks demonstrate broader applicability of the approach.

author: Herrera
title: Knowledge Distillation for Generative Adversarial Network Compression
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks have become instrumental across machine learning applications including synthetic data generation, domain transfer, and super resolution. However, contemporary state-of-the-art variants typically employ tens of millions of parameters, limiting their suitability for deployment in real-time systems and devices with constrained size, weight, and power budgets such as mobile platforms. Prior research has not addressed parameter reduction in GANs. We introduce a compression technique based on knowledge distillation wherein a compact "student" GAN replicates the behavior of a larger "teacher" GAN. Using this distillation approach on Celeb-A, CIFAR-10, and MNIST datasets yields compression ratios of 87:1, 58:1, and 1669:1 respectively while maintaining image quality. Our results indicate an empirical threshold beyond which GAN compression becomes problematic. Notably, within equivalent parameter constraints, compressed GANs demonstrate superior performance relative to those trained via conventional methods. We hypothesize this advantage stems partly from the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, facilitating effective training through alternating gradient descent. Consequently, over-parameterized GAN training combined with subsequent compression yields compact generative models of high fidelity with considerably fewer parameters.

author: Davidson
title: Multiple Perspectives Enhancement for Reliable Re-Identification via Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Re-Identification performance suffers when moving from video-based to image-based scenarios, as conventional approaches depend heavily on temporal cues obtained during video-to-video matching. The transition to single-image queries (Image-To-Video) results in substantial performance degradation. Existing methods mitigate this by transmitting temporal knowledge from video-trained networks to image-trained models. We present a training methodology for conveying richer knowledge learned from multiple visual representations of objects. Our approach—which employs multiple perspectives as training signals within a teacher-student framework—has the student trained on restricted view counts while benefiting from the teacher's exposure to diverse perspectives. The resulting student model surpasses both its teacher and existing Image-To-Video benchmarks substantially: 6.3% mAP improvement on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. We conduct comprehensive evaluation across Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID categories, examining VKD characteristics from both qualitative and quantitative dimensions.

author: Rodriguez
title: Deploying Graph Neural Networks under Formal Privacy Protections
abstract: Graph neural networks have become increasingly common in sensitive domains such as healthcare and medical research, raising significant privacy concerns regarding their trained models. Notably, GNNs remain susceptible to privacy attacks including membership inference, even when attackers possess only black-box query access. This work introduces a framework for privacy-preserving deployment of GNN models within centralized contexts. Given access to a publicly available unlabeled graph, the framework enables release of GNNs trained jointly on public information and private knowledge while maintaining formal privacy safeguards. The approach leverages knowledge distillation alongside two perturbation strategies—random subsampling and noisy labeling—to satisfy stringent privacy guarantees. Theoretical analysis is conducted using the Renyi differential privacy framework. Experimental results demonstrate competitive performance relative to adapted baseline approaches applicable to graph-structured data. Implementation details have been made publicly accessible.

author: Graham
title: Auxiliary-Branch Regularization for Federated Learning via Divergent Client Architectures
abstract: Federated learning systems encounter significant obstacles when training data exhibits heterogeneity and imbalance within client datasets, resulting in local network divergence and unstable global model convergence patterns. We introduce an architectural regularization method that addresses these problems by inserting multiple subsidiary branches into each client model through fusion of global and local subnetwork components at various depths, enabling the chief representation stream of each client model to align with these hybrid subsidiary streams using online knowledge distillation. This approach demonstrates robustness toward global model improvement across heterogeneous non-iid data distributions and integrates seamlessly with multiple federated learning paradigms while avoiding supplementary communication overhead. Comprehensive experimental validation reveals substantial improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency relative to competing approaches. Implementation details are published on the associated project repository.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation Without Access to Training Data for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Techniques for neural network compression have enabled reduction of large models to substantially smaller versions while preserving their predictive capacity. Yet existing methods require availability of the original training corpus, an assumption that frequently fails—whether due to massive scale, or because disclosing such data raises privacy or security challenges, particularly in biometric applications. We propose a technique enabling knowledge distillation without requiring training data, which reduces deep neural networks trained on extensive datasets to a fraction of their initial magnitude by utilizing only supplementary information released alongside the pretrained model. Additionally, we examine various forms of such supplementary information compatible with our approach and analyze the benefits and costs associated with each variant.

author: Mckay
title: Enhancing Compression of Massive Language Models through Data-Independent Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale language models have achieved notable empirical success. Yet these improvements come with substantial computational costs, increased memory requirements, and extended inference latency, limiting deployment on resource-constrained systems. Knowledge distillation has proven effective for reducing the complexity of such expansive models. However, large neural networks frequently overfit to training data and exhibit unstable predictions under marginal shifts in data characteristics. Additionally, when task-specific training data is scarce, student models lack sufficient signal to extract relevant guidance from teacher models. We present a proposed method, a distribution-agnostic distillation technique employing mixup—a straightforward and practical augmentation mechanism—to enhance generalization in compressed models. Specifically, beyond standard examples, the student is trained to match teacher predictions on convex combinations of instance pairs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that, given appropriate assumptions, the method reduces the divergence between test-set and training-set performance. Empirical validation on GLUE shows that our approach yields substantial improvements relative to conventional distillation and competes favorably with other recent methods. Results from low-data regimes and systematic ablations further establish the benefits of this technique.

author: Liu
title: Augmenting CLIP for Multimodal Generation Through Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Vision-language pre-training of two-stream models such as CLIP leverages large quantities of paired image-text data and has demonstrated strong performance across multimodal alignment benchmarks. However, these models lack capacity for generative multimodal tasks because their text encoder is insufficiently powerful. We address this limitation by incorporating a pre-trained language model into a dual-stream vision-language architecture through vision-language knowledge distillation, thereby enabling multimodal generation. This approach is highly efficient in terms of both data and computational requirements relative to training from initialization. Empirical findings demonstrate competitive zero-shot results on generative multimodal benchmarks, including image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. Notably, the method achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on VQAv2, exceeding the prior zero-shot state-of-the-art with 7× parameter reduction. The method additionally preserves the pre-trained language model's original text understanding and generation capacities, enabling effective deployment on both multimodal and unimodal objectives.

author: Mason
title: Acquiring Lightweight Networks Through Feature Space Alignment
abstract: Practical deployment of convolutional neural networks remains challenging due to substantial memory footprint and computational demands that limit real-world use on resource-constrained platforms. Knowledge distillation provides a mechanism to refine a compact student network by extracting pedagogical signals from an established teacher network. Previous approaches in this paradigm incorporated supplementary fully-connected components to connect intermediate representations between teacher and student architectures, introducing numerous additional learnable parameters. This work presents an alternative strategy: transferring information across the student-teacher relationship while avoiding the introduction of extra trainable variables. We conceptualize this transfer mechanism through a feature embedding lens. By implementing a locality-aware similarity objective, compressed feature representations in the student are shaped to capture the fundamental characteristics inherent in the corresponding expanded feature spaces of the teacher. The resulting efficient model thereby sustains comparable accuracy to the original teacher. Formal justification demonstrates reduced operational expenditure relative to competing approaches. Comparative evaluation against standard benchmarks and pretrained architectures demonstrates advantages in terms of memory and computational efficiency over existing teacher-student knowledge transfer methodologies.

author: White
title: Compressing Lightweight Generative Adversarial Networks via Knowledge Transfer for Cross-domain Image Synthesis
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks have found widespread application across numerous image-to-image translation tasks, yet their deployment on portable computing hardware remains challenging due to substantial computational and memory requirements. Network compression approaches in existing literature have concentrated on recognition objectives rather than generation tasks. Motivated by knowledge distillation principles, we train a student generator with reduced parameters that learns both coarse and fine-grained representations from a larger teacher generator. To strengthen the student generator's performance, a student discriminator is incorporated to evaluate divergences among genuine images and outputs from both student and teacher generators. This configuration enables an adversarial training regime for jointly optimizing the student generator alongside the student discriminator. Results from qualitative and quantitative evaluation on established benchmarks indicate the proposed method successfully produces compact generative models achieving competitive performance.

author: Gaines
title: Differentiable Neural Architecture Search for Specialized BERT Compression Across Distinct Natural Language Tasks
abstract: Pre-trained language models including BERT have demonstrated strong performance on diverse natural language processing benchmarks. Their considerable parameter counts, however, impede deployment in scenarios demanding rapid inference under strict computational constraints. Previous compression approaches reduce BERT to smaller models in a task-agnostic manner, applying identical compression across all downstream applications. Recognizing the potential of tailoring compression to individual tasks, we introduce a compression method employing differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically produce task-specific compact BERT variants for targeted applications. Our approach integrates task-oriented knowledge distillation loss as guidance during search alongside an efficiency-aware loss functioning as search constraints, balancing performance and computational efficiency in the compressed models. Testing across multiple NLP benchmarks reveals that the resulting task-specialized models achieve 12.7x to 29.3x speedups relative to BERT during inference and 11.5x to 17.0x reductions in parameter count, while sustaining performance parity.

author: Harrell
title: Heterogeneous Device Participation in Federated Learning: A Strategy for Inclusive Model Training
abstract: Federated learning represents a critical approach to constructing distributed models while maintaining privacy across decentralized datasets. Standard FL algorithms typically presuppose that participating clients can execute identical global model training procedures. Practical deployments, however, present heterogeneous client hardware with varying computational resources. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of large architectures such as BERT in modern AI systems, integrating them into federated settings with resource-constrained clients remains challenging. Naive approaches—either excluding limited-capacity devices or employing undersized models for universal deployment—introduce complications including missing data from excluded participants and reduced accuracy stemming from architectural constraints or information loss. We introduce a participant-inclusive federated framework that simultaneously trains models of varying capacities suited to individual client specifications: larger architectures on capable devices, compact variants on resource-limited ones. A corresponding knowledge-sharing mechanism enables effective parameter transfer between local models of disparate sizes. This design ensures comprehensive client involvement throughout federated training while maintaining model quality through sufficient capacity. Additionally, momentum-based knowledge distillation facilitates superior parameter transfer from expanded models executing on capable devices to condensed models on constrained infrastructure. Validation across diverse real-world datasets demonstrates that our approach successfully achieves competitive performance when training with clients exhibiting heterogeneous computational constraints under the federated framework.

author: Evans
title: Condensed Language Models for Translation Evaluation
abstract: Machine translation and cross-lingual generation systems increasingly employ learned evaluation metrics such as COMET and BLEURT, which formulate assessment as a regression task leveraging embeddings from multilingual foundational models including XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT. However, related research indicates optimal performance requires larger model architectures, presenting deployment challenges. We examine the relationship between multilingual coverage and model parameters using RemBERT, a leading multilingual language model, drawing on datasets from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. Through systematic experiments, we demonstrate that model dimensions constrain multilingual generalization across languages, and propose knowledge distillation as a solution utilizing artificial data and single-teacher-to-multiple-student transfer across linguistically related settings. The approach achieves up to 10.5% gains relative to baseline fine-tuning while matching 92.6% of RemBERT's effectiveness with one-third the parameter count.

author: Fowler
title: Leveraging Teacher Networks for Self-Supervised Visual Feature Learning in Compact Models
abstract: Self-supervised learning on compact architectures presents significant challenges. Empirical observations indicate that large models benefit substantially from contrastive self-supervised approaches, whereas small models struggle with these methods. We introduce a framework utilizing knowledge transfer from a larger teacher network to a smaller student network within a self-supervised setting to overcome this limitation. Rather than optimizing directly on unlabeled instances, the student encoder is trained to replicate the similarity score distributions that the teacher produces across multiple samples. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach substantially enhances downstream performance on compact architectures. Relative to self-supervised baselines, our method achieves top-1 accuracy improvements of 25.4 percentage points (from 42.2% to 67.6%) for EfficientNet-B0 and 31.9 percentage points (from 36.3% to 68.2%) for MobileNet-v3-Large when evaluated on ImageNet-1k.

author: Lynch
title: Knowledge Transfer from Visual to Wearable Sensor Modalities for Activity Recognition
abstract: Multimodal architectures have demonstrated improvements in human activity recognition (HAR), yet wearable platforms like smartwatches present severe constraints on computational capacity, limiting their ability to execute such demanding approaches. This work proposes an end-to-end framework enabling distillation from visual into sensor-based models, wherein accelerometer signals alone are sufficient during inference on resource-limited edge devices. The approach maintains the performance characteristics of expensive multimodal systems while substantially decreasing processing overhead. To preserve local temporal dependencies and leverage visual feature extraction, time-series sensor measurements are first encoded into two-dimensional spatial representations using Gramian Angular Field transformation. The framework employs ResNet18 as the teacher network and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as the student network. A specialized loss function incorporating distance and angular semantic relationships is introduced to address domain-specific variations arising from the vision-to-sensor conversion. Validation across UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD benchmarks demonstrates both the viability and competitive efficacy of the proposed approach for deployment on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Efficient Novel View Synthesis via Knowledge Transfer from Neural Radiance Fields to Deep Light Field Networks
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have demonstrated substantial capacity for encoding intricate scenes through learned representations, yet their computational demands during rendering remain prohibitive. Rendering each pixel typically necessitates hundreds of forward evaluations through the NeRF network. While previous work has concentrated on minimizing the count of sample points needed, the challenge of sequential sampling persists. By contrast, Neural Light Fields (NeLF) offer a fundamentally more efficient pathway to synthesizing novel views—a single network evaluation per pixel suffices, eliminating the need for ray-marching procedures. This paper proposes training a deep residual MLP with 88 layers as a light field model. Success in learning such a deep architecture depends critically on access to ample training examples, which we obtain by distilling knowledge from an existing NeRF through synthetic data generation. Evaluation across diverse synthetic and realistic environments demonstrates substantial computational and visual improvements. Our method achieves 26-35x FLOP reduction per camera ray alongside 28-31x improvement in rendering speed, while simultaneously producing superior output quality (1.4-2.8 dB higher average PSNR) relative to NeRF, requiring no specialized hardware acceleration.

author: Farmer
title: Computationally Lightweight 3D Detection via Student-Teacher Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Current 3D object detectors based on pillars and voxels face substantial computational burdens despite recent advances. This work investigates knowledge distillation as a path toward reducing computational requirements in 3D detection tasks. Given the scarcity of established distillation frameworks, we initially examine strategies for obtaining student models that balance performance gains against inference costs, drawing on both architectural pruning and resolution scaling. Subsequently, we construct an evaluation framework to test KD techniques originally designed for 2D detection when applied to 3D scenarios across six distinct teacher-student configurations. We introduce a refined distillation strategy with an enhanced logit KD component that concentrates on selectively important positions identified by teacher confidence scores, alongside weight inheritance mechanisms that guide student networks in acquiring feature extraction capabilities from their teachers. Comprehensive evaluation employs the Waymo benchmark. The strongest configuration attains 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, outperforming the teacher while consuming merely 44% of its computational budget. The fastest variant executes at 51 FPS on NVIDIA A100 hardware, delivering 2.2× throughput improvement over PointPillar while maintaining superior performance. Implementation details are publicly released.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring segmentation knowledge across modality dimensions: Multi-modal instruction of single-modality networks
abstract: Multi-modality medical image segmentation has gained considerable attention because combining information across imaging channels consistently yields improved accuracy relative to single-modality approaches. In clinical practice, however, obtaining multiple imaging channels presents significant logistical barriers: scanner availability constraints, physician staffing limitations, economic considerations, and patient time demands typically restrict acquisition to a single modality. We introduce a framework for conveying learned representations from a multi-modal network (teacher) toward a single-modality network (student) through knowledge distillation. This work adapts the general distillation paradigm by having the student network learn from a reduced input space (1 modality) while the teacher accesses the full space (n modalities). We evaluate our methodology on brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS 2018 dataset across several network configurations. Results demonstrate that the student network successfully acquires knowledge from the teacher, consistently surpassing the conventional mono-modal baseline in segmentation performance.

author: Osborne
title: Transfer of Learning from Sophisticated Networks to Clinical Applications
abstract: Computational Phenotyping research has expanded significantly due to proliferation in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR), creating both prospects and pressing demands for identifying actionable representations and disease-related patterns through data-driven methods. While Deep Learning models deliver strong results for prediction tasks in computational phenotyping, they encounter difficulties with interpretability—a critical factor for clinicians making treatment decisions. This work presents a novel knowledge-distillation technique designed to capture interpretable phenotype features that sustain prediction robustness while replicating the performance achieved by deep learning systems. The proposed method employs Gradient Boosting Trees to extract interpretable features from sophisticated models including Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory networks. Comprehensive evaluation using authentic clinical time-series data demonstrates that the approach achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of deep learning models, while simultaneously offering interpretable phenotypes suitable for guiding clinical practice.

author: Moreno
title: Awareness of Sensor Constraints in Rapid Autonomous Flight Through Obstructed Spaces
abstract: Neural network-based control strategies have recently surpassed traditional model-based planning approaches for enabling unmanned quadrotor vehicles to traverse densely obstructed spaces while minimizing flight duration. A critical limitation of these techniques is their failure to account for perception constraints—particularly significant for vision-centric navigation, where the camera's restricted angular coverage and the dynamical underactuation of quadrotors pose fundamental challenges. We introduce a learning-based framework that integrates perception constraints with agile autonomous flight in obstacle-rich settings. This framework merges supervised learning with reinforcement learning via a privileged cheating-based training paradigm. Initially, RL is applied to develop a teacher policy that incorporates perception awareness and utilizes full-state observations to achieve minimum-time trajectories in cluttered spaces. Subsequently, this teacher's expertise is transferred via imitation learning to a student policy operating exclusively with camera input, enforcing tight integration of visual perception and control actions. The resulting approach demonstrates substantial improvements in both computational efficiency (achieving 10-fold speedup) and mission completion likelihood. Validation occurs through hardware-in-the-loop experimental simulation protocols.

author: Smith
title: Compressing and Refining General Language Models for Domain-Specific Applications Through Vocabulary Extension and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: General-purpose pretrained language models have demonstrated substantial performance across numerous NLP benchmarks. When deployed within specialized domains, however, these models encounter significant domain shift, creating practical difficulties for both fine-tuning procedures and inference serving due to memory footprint and computational speed requirements. This work proposes a unified framework for constructing compact, expedited, and performant pretrained language models tailored to particular domains. The approach involves modifying readily available general pretrained models through task-agnostic distillation targeted at the domain of interest. We introduce domain-specialized vocabulary augmentation during the modification phase and leverage corpus-level occurrence frequency to automatically establish the volume of added vocabulary terms. Subsequently, we investigate multiple approaches for reducing the size of large pretrained models applicable to specialized domains. Evaluation takes place on biomedical and computer science corpora. Our findings indicate the approach surpasses BERT BASE performance on domain-specific benchmarks while achieving 3.3x reduction in model size and 5.1x improvement in inference speed relative to BERT BASE. Implementation code and model weights are accessible at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Teacher-Student Training for Compact Highway-Based Acoustic Models
abstract: Recent advances in neural network-based acoustic modeling have substantially improved speech recognition performance. Yet neural architectures typically require considerably more parameters than traditional Gaussian mixture models, making deployment on resource-constrained hardware challenging. We previously developed highway depth-gated feedforward networks for acoustic modeling and demonstrated they match recognition rates of standard deep networks while using far fewer parameters. This work extends that approach by applying teacher-student knowledge distillation, where a lightweight highway model learns from a larger high-performing network during training. We additionally examine sequence training combined with speaker adaptation under the teacher-student framework. Experiments on the AMI meeting corpus show that this methodology substantially boosts recognition performance of highway models with under 0.8 million parameters, substantially reducing the performance differential relative to standard deep networks containing 30 million parameters.
